10: Woe to those who make unjust laws, and who in writing have written injustice, to oppress the poor in judgment, and to do violence to the cause of the humble of my people, that widows might be their prey, and that they might plunder the orphans. What will you do in the day of visitation, and of the calamity coming from afar? To whose help will you flee? And where will you leave your glory? that you may not be bowed down under the chain, and fall with the slain. For all these his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Most think that these things too are still said against the ten tribes which dwelt in Samaria, because they joined these as well to their former crimes. To us, however, it seems that the prophetic word cries out against the judges of the tribe of Judah and of Jerusalem, namely the scribes and the δευτερωτὰς, because they wrote unjust laws against the law of God, and by their traditions overturned the truth of judgment. For when God says: Honor your father and mother (Exod 20:12), they on the contrary taught sons to say to their parents: Whatever gift comes from me will profit you, so that they do not honor father and mother (Matt 15:5-6; Mark 7:11), and other things like these. And they wrote these most evil laws for this purpose, to oppress the poor and the humble of the people, to make plunder of widows and to despoil orphans. They are asked what they will do when the day either of captivity or of judgment has come, and of the calamity coming from afar, which was foretold long before. To whose help, he says, will you flee, when you have offended God, who is the true helper, and where will you leave your glory? For riches will not profit in the day of wrath, to keep the Assyrian from leading you in chains into the enemy's land, to keep you from falling in battle (Prov 11:4). And finally, just as in the preceding passages he had often said against Samaria: For all these his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out, he speaks so against Judah too, because the final captivity is not the end of their evil, but even in the enemy's land the sword of the Lord will pursue them. According to the anagogy, every heretic writes iniquity in order to deceive the poor and humble of the people and to despoil widows and orphans. For the rich man, of whom we read: A man's own riches are the redemption of his soul (Prov 13:8), does not endure threats, is not quickly caught by them. But the poor man, and he who is humble and small among the peoples, is quickly made to stumble by them. The widow too, who has lost God her husband, and the orphan who has lost his father the Creator, of whom it is written: You have forsaken God who begot you, and have forgotten God your nourisher (Deut 32:18), are easily tripped up. What then will they do in the day of judgment, when they have deceived so many, and of the calamity coming from afar? For just as it is said to the righteous man: The word is near, in your mouth and in your heart (Rom 10:8); and in another place: The kingdom of God is within you (Luke 17:21); so the calamity of the heretics will come from afar, prepared for them over a long time. To whom will they flee for refuge, when the God they have is a fiction? To whom will they hand over their glory, when everything is feigned? Nor will they be able to escape the chain with which they have bound very many. Hence also in the vision of the valley of Zion, which, forsaking the height of God, has been deceived by heretical lowliness, it is said of the teachers of knowledge falsely so called: All your princes have fled, and those who were captured were harshly bound (Isa 22:3); and that they fall with the slain one by one, and perish themselves in the slaughter of others, and though they suffer many things, and the day of visitation has come, their destruction is not their end: but they are ever to tremble at the hand of the Lord hanging over them. Up to this point is God's threat against the ten and the two tribes, that is, against Samaria and Jerusalem, which began among the people while Ahaz was still reigning: of these, two and a half tribes were taken captive under him, and the rest under Hezekiah, who succeeded Ahaz in the kingdom (2 Kgs 16:17). The following prophecy is written against the Assyrians.

Woe to them that make wicked laws. Here he begins to threaten against foreign enemies who persecute them bodily: and first, against those who lay waste, second, against those who rejoice in this laying waste: in the year that king Achaz died (Isa 14:28). The first of these is divided into two: in the first, he threatens against the Assyrians who were taking the ten tribes captive and afflicting the two tribes; in the second, against the Babylonians who take the two tribes captive: the burden of Babylon (ch. 13). The first of these is divided into three: in the first, he threatens the destruction of the enemies; in the second, he promises the restoration of the people: and there shall come forth (ch. 11); in the third, he places their thanksgiving: I will give thanks (ch. 12).

And this chapter is divided into two parts: in the first, he threatens against the princes of the two tribes, who trusted in the help of the Assyrians, namely Achaz, under whom this vision was written, as is read in 2 Kings 16:7; in the second, against the Assyrians themselves: woe to the Assyrian (Isa 10:4). However, some begin chapter 10 there, and then it would be easier, because this part would thus not be distinguished from the preceding chapter.

The first of these is divided into two: in the first, the threat is set out; in the second, the preparation of further punishment is shown: in all these things (Isa 10:4). The first is divided into two: in the first, he denounces their fault, in the second, he threatens punishment: what will you do? (Isa 10:3). He denounces the fault of the princes as to two things. As to perverse lawgiving: woe to them that make wicked laws, in as far as the law is established by the decree of the prince, and when they write, in as far as it is confirmed in writing: for they, not knowing the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God (Rom 10:3); why do your disciples transgress (Matt 15:2).

For the robbers have not vanished from the old high forests to the west of the great city. The thieves have not vanished; they have grown so large that they are invisible. You do not see the word "Asia" written across a map of that neighbourhood; nor do you see the word "Thief" written across the countrysides of England; though it is really written in equally large letters. I know men governing despotically great stretches of that country, whose every step in life has been such that a slip would have sent them to Dartmoor; but they trod along the high hard wall between right and wrong, the wall as sharp as a swordedge, as softly and craftily and lightly as a cat. The vastness of their silent violence itself obscured what they were at; if they seem to stand for the rights of property it is really because they have so often invaded them. And if they do not break the laws, it is only because they make them.
Alarms and Discursions, The Steward of the Chiltern Hundreds (1910)

Second, as to the intention of oppressing those who are powerless, either because of poverty: the poor, or because of low rank: humble: they crush as the dust (Amos 2:7); or because of weakness of sex: widows; or because of age: orphans. Above: they judge not for orphans (Isa 1:23).

[Christ] said to Peter, the prince of the apostles, "Simon, [son] of John, do you love me more than these?" He answered, "Lord, you know I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs." He asked him a second time, "Simon [son] of John, do you love me?" He answered, "Yes, Lord, you know I love you." He said to him, "Feed my sheep." And he ordered him to feed his sheep a third time, and in Peter he enjoined this office on all of us, diligently to feed the sheep of the Lord, that on the day of his visitation we may, for our toil and watchfulness, receive what he promised us in the gospel, saying, Father, I wish that where I am, there also shall be my minister. Let us look to the promises and rewards; then in an attitude of faith we will more easily stand all our pains, walking as the Lord himself walked, who is the one promising the rewards.

"What shall we do in the day of visitation?" One of the prophets terrifies me [with this question], whether that of the righteous sentence of God against us or that upon the mountains and hills, of which we have heard. Whatever and whenever it may be, he will reason with us and oppose us and set before us those bitter accusers, which are our sins, contrasting our wrongdoings with our benefits, striking thought with thought, scrutinizing action with action and calling us to account for the image that has been blurred and spoiled by wickedness. He will finally lead us away self-convicted and self-condemned, no longer able to say that we are being unjustly treated—a thought that is able even here sometimes to console in their condemnation those who are suffering.

What will you do? Here he threatens punishment, and first, he takes away the remedy of escape. And this is threefold: confidence in their own power: what will you do in the day of visitation, and of the calamity which comes from afar, as to the fortifying of their enemies or as to the prediction of the prophets: what will you do in the solemn day, in the day of the feast of the Lord? (Hos 9:5). Who can stand before the face of his indignation? (Nah 1:6). Second, as to the friendship of the powerful: to whom will you flee for help? Behold there is no help for me in myself, and my familiar friends also are departed from me (Job 6:13). Third, as to the glory of riches: and where will you leave your glory, as if to say: which will not profit you. What has pride profited us? Or what advantage has the boasting of riches brought us? (Wis 5:8).

Second, he expresses the manner of punishment, and first, the punishment of captivity: that you be not bowed down under, above: and the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be humbled (Isa 2:17); second, of killing: and fall with the slain: all of them slain, fallen by the sword (Ezek 32:24).

In all these things. Here the preparation of further punishment is set out: this is explained as above.

And Sennacherib also said thus:—I will go up to the summit of the mountains and to the shoulders of Lebanon. I will dig and drink water and will dry up with my horses’ hoofs all the deep rivers. And because he thus exalted himself, Isaiah again said concerning him:—Why does the axe boast itself against him that cutteth with it, or the saw exalt itself against him that saweth with it, or the rod lift itself up against him that wieldeth it? For thou, Sennacherib, art the axe in the hands of Him that cuts, and thou art the saw in the hands of Him that saws, and the rod in the hand of Him that wields thee for chastisement, and thou art the staff for smiting. Thou art sent against the fickle people, and again thou art ordained against the stubborn people, that thou mayest carry away the captivity and take the spoil; and thou hast made them as the mire of the streets for all men and for all the Gentiles. And when thou hast done all these things, why art thou exalted against Him Who holds thee, and why dost thou boast against Him Who saws with thee, and why hast thou reviled the holy city? and hast said to the children of Jerusalem:—Can your God deliver you from my hand? And thou hast dared to say:—Who is the Lord that He shall deliver you from my hands?

Woe to Assur, the rod of my fury, and he is the staff; in their hand is my indignation. Against a deceitful nation I will send him, and against the people of my fury I will give him charge, to take spoils and to seize prey, and to make it a thing trodden down like the mire of the streets. But he does not think so, and his heart does not reckon so, but his heart will be set on crushing, and on the slaughter of very many nations. For he says: Are not my princes all of them kings? Is it not: as Carchemish, so Chalanno and as Arpad, so Hamath? Is it not: as Damascus, so Samaria? As my hand found the kingdoms of the idol, so also their images from Jerusalem and from Samaria. Shall I not, as I did to Samaria and to her idols, so do to Jerusalem and to her images? Let us set down in this place the translation of the Seventy, which disagrees with the Hebrew in very many things. LXX: Woe to the Assyrians: the rod of my fury is he, in their hands; my wrath I will send against a lawless nation, and to my people I will give command to make spoils and prey, and to trample the cities, and to lay them in the dust: but he did not so think, and did not so reckon; but his mind is to crush, and to destroy very many nations. And if they say to him: You alone are prince, he will answer: I have not taken the region which is above Babylon, and Chalane, where the tower was built. But I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria: as I have taken these, so I will take all kingdoms. Howl, you carved images in Jerusalem and Samaria; for as I did to Samaria and to her idols, so I will do to Jerusalem and to her images. First it must be known that in the Hebrew it does not have Chalane, but CHALANNO (כלנו). For the last letter of this name is not IOD, as they supposed, but VAU, letters which differ from each other only in size. Now the tower was built in the plain of Shinar, in which were Erech, Accad, and Chalanne, and Babylon, which received its name from the confusion of tongues (Gen 11). Arabia, moreover, is not found in the Hebrew, but Hamath, which the Syrians to this day call Epiphania. Howl too, you carved images in Jerusalem, they added of their own. And what is written above: If they say to him, You alone are prince, he will answer, I have not taken the region this one and that one, but I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria, suggests this sense: When, he says, those who have been taken captive say to the Assyrian, You are prince of all, he, still feeling himself to be weak, will answer: How do you call me prince, when I have taken only Arabia and Damascus and Samaria, and have not yet brought under my power the nations set far off beyond Babylon? But as I took Arabia, Damascus and Samaria, so I will lay all kingdoms beneath me. Let us pass to the Hebrew, and briefly note what seems right to us. Woe to the Assyrian, that is, Sennacherib, because he is the rod and the staff of my fury, for in his hand is my indignation, and through him I will strike a most deceitful nation, which has always limped between me and the idols, which lied that it would do my precepts; and against the people of my fury I will command him to despoil it and plunder it, and to reduce it to dust, and to trample it like the mire of the streets, that is, to strike it and not kill it, to wound it and not take away its life. But he went beyond the measure of my anger, and raged not only against Israel, against which he had been directed, but against very many nations, so as to crush all the kingdoms round about, and his sword raged even to the slaughter of very many nations. For, lifted up into pride, he dared to say this: My captains are kings of other nations, and, being subject to me, they will rule all nations. As I took Carchemish, so I took Chalanno too; as Arpad, so I gained Hamath too; as Damascus, so I subjected Samaria to myself too. As I have put under my feet the other kingdoms which served the worship of idols, so I will subject to my power Jerusalem too, and Samaria, in which are the same idols. As I took Samaria with its idols, so I will take Jerusalem too, because it worships the same gods. For Carchemish, however, the Seventy, adding of their own, translated the region beyond Babylon, and Chalane where the tower was built, leaving out Arpad altogether. But according to their translation, and with the freedom of tropology, provided it is pious, from what he says, and I will give command to my people to make spoils and prey, and to trample the cities, and to lay them in the dust, we can say this too: that the Lord daily commands his people to reduce to dust the cities of the adversaries, which are raised up against the knowledge of God and have been built by the heretics with enormous labor, and to show that they are nothing. And he, understanding the weakness of the human heart, and that, surrounded as he is with mortal flesh, he cannot have a perfect victory of the virtues nor take all the nations, though others admire him and say: You alone are prince, will answer them: There are many things that I ought to destroy, and have not yet been able to destroy: I know that I do not know. And although I have overcome many arguments of the adversaries, yet there are very many which are still to be overcome. And at the same time, in hope of what is to come, from those which he has overcome he promises himself the victory over the rest as well. Now the images of Jerusalem and of Samaria are bidden to howl: not the things themselves which were fashioned, but those who fashioned them: μετωνυμικῶς, those who made them, by the things that were made: so that not only those who have fabricated idols in the heresies, but those who in the Church through ignorance defend a lie for the truth, may testify by howling and penitence that they have erred.

Woe to the Assyrian. In this part, he threatens against the Assyrians themselves, and this is divided into two parts: in the first part the threat against the enemies who oppress them is set out; in the second, the strengthening of the oppressed people: therefore, thus says the Lord (Isa 10:24). The first of these is divided into three: in the first, he denounces their fault; in the second, he threatens punishment: therefore the sovereign Lord, the Lord of hosts, shall send (Isa 10:16); in the third, he shows the effect of the punishment: and he shall run away (Isa 10:18). And their fault consists in transgression of precept or in abuse of authority; hence, the first part is divided into three: in the first, their commission of authority is set out; in the second, their abuse of authority: but he shall not take it so (Isa 10:7); in the third, the vainglory of the abuser: and it shall come to pass, that when the Lord shall have performed (Isa 10:12).

Concerning the first, he does three things: first, the office of scourging is committed to the Assyrians; second, he designates the one who is deserving of scourges: I will send him to a deceitful nation (Isa 10:6); third, he sets out the manner of scourging: to take away the spoils (Isa 10:6). Concerning the first, he designates three things: the one who scourges: woe, it nears you, the Assyrian, you who are the rod of my anger; the power of scourging: the staff, by which I myself scourge, is in their hands, that is, their power, that is, in execution; and the scourging: my indignation is fulfilled through them, below: the Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers, that struck the people in wrath with an incurable wound (Isa 14:5–6).

I will send him to a deceitful nation. Here he describes the one who is deserving of scourges, both as to the fault: a deceitful nation, because it does not keep its promise: all that the Lord has spoken, we will do (Exod 19:8); and as to the sentence, the people of my wrath, that is, whom I have already judged fit to be punished, I will send, I will inspire you to be fit to be punished: the Lord said to me: go up to this land, and destroy it (2 Kgs 18:25); to, that is, against.

To take away. Here he sets out the mode of scourging as to the taking away of their things: take away spoils; as to detention, lay hold; as to the oppression of men: tread them down like the mire, for their baseness: I shall bring them to naught, like the mire in the streets (Ps 17:43).

But he shall not take it so. Here the abuse of the power conceded to the Assyrian is set out, insofar as he exceeded the ends of the mandate; and first, his intention is set out; second, the motive of his intention is set out: for he shall say (Isa 10:8). Concerning the first, he does two things: first, he dismisses the fixed measure of the mandate, both as to the judgment of reason: but he shall not take it so, and as to the intention of the heart: his heart shall not think so, that is, he will assess the punishment; second, he increases the punishment both as to manner: to grind to pieces, that is, utterly destroy everything, and as to number: nations not a few, but rather many, not only those to whom he was sent: you have devised confusion to your house, you have cut off many people, and your soul has sinned (Hab 2:10).

For he shall say. Here his motive is set out; and first, he argues, second, he concludes: so shall I do to Jerusalem and her images (Isa 10:11). Concerning the first, he first argues the servitude of kings: are not my princes as so many kings? He shall triumph over kings, and princes shall be his laughingstock (Hab 1:10).
Second, the subjugation of cities: is not Calano as Charcamis, below: for of a truth, O Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have laid waste lands, and their countries (Isa 37:18).

Long ago, indeed, when the former people sinned, Judah fell away from religion and fashioned "graven images in Jerusalem," and he who was called Israel did so "in Samaria". But if now too someone should consider, out of the multitude of those sinners who are gathered together, he will not be reluctant to say that each one who makes for himself a god — whatever he reckons to be good — and serves sin, is accursed, making a "graven image" and casting a work of the craftsman's hands and setting it up in secret; for in the secret place of the heart we make many idols, if we sin. Hence the word teaches us to do penance and to "wail over the graven images" and idols that are "in Jerusalem and Samaria". And if indeed we sin, we who desire to be of the Church, we make "graven images in Jerusalem"; but if those who are established outside the Church — as heretics — sin, they make "idols in Samaria". Nevertheless God, according to his goodness, calls all to penance, saying: "Wail, you graven images in Jerusalem and in Samaria; for just as I did to Samaria and to the works of its hands, so will I do also to Jerusalem and to its idols". He threatens that whatever things "he did to the Samaritans" he will do also to those who are of the Church.

Third, the destruction of idols: how my hand has found the kingdoms of the idol: wonderingly, as if to say: how was it that their gods did not resist me: who are they among all the gods of the nations that have delivered their country out of my hand, that God may deliver Jerusalem out of my hand? (2 Kgs 18:35).

So shall I do to Jerusalem and her images. Here he concludes first, from the nations to the entire people of Israel: so also their images of Jerusalem, and of Samaria; second, from the ten tribes to the two: shall I not, as I have done to Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her images? He speaks the truth concerning Samaria, because they worshipped idols, but Ezechias had removed the idols from Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18:4); also perhaps some idols secretly remained, which he found in the part of the city that Sobna the scribe handed over to him; or he calls the ark and the other things that adorned the temple images: behold the house of Judah is like all other nations (Ezek 25:8).

"But when the Lord has finished doing all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, he will bring judgment upon the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, and upon the loftiness of the glory of his eyes". We are taught what shall come to be for our enemy the devil, whom the prophecy has now called a certain "great mind". For just as "the serpent was wiser than all the beasts that are upon the earth", and "the sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their generation", and "the steward of iniquity acted wisely" according to a wisdom that is not good, in the same way this one, who is figuratively called "the prince of the Assyrians", is a "great mind", and one may marvel at the greatness of his "mind"; which he has misused for the instructing of the wise of this world, who compose the falsehood of their sects with every appearance of truth and with all their power, and put it on display. "When" therefore "God has done all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem" and has rendered those things which have been promised to the just, then "he will bring judgment upon the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, and upon the loftiness of the glory of his eyes". The word knows him to be "wise" as to "high things", and that the beginning of his ruin took its start from being puffed up. Hence, if we too have been puffed up, we "fall into the judgment of the devil", "into" which "the devil himself fell".

And it shall be, when the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, I will visit upon the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assur, and upon the glory of the haughtiness of his eyes. For he said: By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood, and I have removed the bounds of the peoples, and I have plundered their princes, and like a mighty one I have pulled down those who sat on high; and my hand has found the strength of the peoples as a nest; and as eggs are gathered which have been left, so I have gathered all the earth, and there was none who moved a wing, or opened the mouth, or chirped. For fruit the Seventy translated sense, or great mind. After the captivity of Samaria, and the victory of the Assyrians, and the threat against Jerusalem, that, because it had imitated the images of Samaria, it must be struck with a like sentence, the Prophet now speaks against the Assyrian himself, who was lifted up into pride and thought that what he conquered was the work of his own strength. For the Assyrian, boasting in the swelling of his heart, said that by the strength of his hand he had conquered all the nations, and by incredible wisdom had taken possession of the bounds of all. And according to the Seventy he was of such power that he overthrew from their foundations the cities of warlike men, and seized the whole world like a nest, and made it his prey like eggs abandoned by their mothers. And because he had once taken a metaphor from birds, from the nest and the eggs, he kept it in the rest, so as to say: There was none who moved a wing, or opened the mouth, or chirped. So great, he says, was the terror of my strength and victory, that the conquered did not freely utter even weeping and groaning. There are those who think these things are said generally against the kingdom of the Assyrians: that after the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that is, after Jerusalem has been overthrown, the empire of the Assyrians is destroyed. To me, however, from what follows, the threat seems to be properly against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians. And what he says: After the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, signifies not the overthrow of the city but its siege, when Rabshakeh, Sennacherib's general, came and did the things which the same Prophet records in later chapters (Isa 37:17). According to tropology, when Samaria and Jerusalem have borne the wrath of the Lord, and have perceived that they erred in fabricating idols, then will the great mind be destroyed, the Assyrian, who was puffed up into such pride against the Lord that he reckoned that all things would yield to his wisdom, and that any lofty doctrines, even those fortified by the art of dialectic, were to be shaken and utterly destroyed: so much so that, like the chicks of birds, they would not be able to rise up on high, and, not yet quickened, would be without sense and torpid, which the example of the eggs shows; and that he would not hear anyone so much as mutter or move his tongue against the reason and strength of his discourse.

And it shall come to pass. Here he denounces his pride. And first, his proud boasting is set out, second, the occasion of his boasting: for he has said (Isa 10:13); third, the rebuke of the boaster: shall the axe boast? (Isa 10:15). Therefore he says: and it shall come to pass, that when the Lord shall have performed all his works in mount Zion, namely, the punishments by which he wishes to correct them, the proud heart, as to presumption of his doing, and the glory of the haughtiness of his eyes, as to his vainglory over his deeds, above: the lofty eyes of man are humbled (Isa 2:11).

But let us also see how great his self-inflation is, that we may guard against it and not permit him to speak true things over us. What, then, does he say? "By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will take away the borders of the nations". He reckons that by his own might he is able to accomplish in us whatever he wishes. And truly, if we are conquered and after these words we sin — if after the Church we go again into the circus and to the horse-races and to the assemblies of the Gentiles — what else happens than that he possesses us as those he has overcome? And what the devil said, "By my strength I will act," comes to pass in us who sin, as he threatened. And also, if we commit fornication after chastity of long duration, after much holiness, what else happens than that he is proved to have spoken true things over us, he who said: "By my strength I will act"? But let us look at what else this boaster promises. "And by the wisdom of my understanding I will take away the borders of the nations". He promises some kind of "wisdom" or other — the wisdom of which the prophet also speaks: "there is a certain alien wisdom in them". There is a certain "wisdom estranged" from the truth, which God destroys. Having this, he reckons himself to be "wise" and says: "By the wisdom of my understanding I will take away the borders of the nations, and I will feed upon their strength". For his working has reached to all the "nations", but the Savior, sending his words into all the "nations", rescues those who by the devil were held captive among all the "nations". "And I will feed upon their strength". He threatens that he will go to plunder our "strength" and to hand it over to those who war against us. And truly one may see him doing this to certain people. For when someone is conquered by the devil and handed over to demons, to most wicked spirits, to the opposing powers, what else has happened than that he who had said, "and I will feed upon their strength", has taken our "strength" and "fed upon" us? "And I will shake the cities that are inhabited". This too the devil threatens: he perceives that the "cities" — the churches of God built in Christ the Lord — are "inhabited", and he gives out that he will "shake" these. And frequently indeed he has shaken the "inhabited cities" with persecutions, frequently he has shaken them with scandals. But let us strive, having our "foundation upon the rock", to become such that this one who says, "I will shake the cities that are inhabited", may not be able to "move" us by his storms nor by his adverse spirits, but that we may persevere steadfast against all things that may befall, inasmuch as we have our edifice "upon the rock," Jesus "Christ", "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

SUCH was their position. While those on the side of the opposing rebel power were either daemons, or vile spirits immersed more or less in wickedness, with the cunning ruler of them all the mighty daemon, who first failed of their reverence of the Divinity and fell from their own portion, when envy of man's salvation drew them the contrary way, plotting with all sorts of evil devices against all the nations, and even against the Lord's portion in their jealousy of the good. It is this godless and unholy scheme of the great Daemon, which the prophetic spirit in Isaiah reproves in this way, saying:

"13. I will act in strength, and in the wisdom of understanding I will take away the boundaries of the nations, and will diminish their strength, 14. and I will shake inhabited cities. And the whole inhabited world I will take in my hand as a nest, and I will take them even as eggs that have been left; and none shall escape me or say me nay."

These are the words of God's antagonist, boasting in the strength of his wickedness, as he threatens to steal and obliterate the divisions of the nations delivered by the Most High to the angels, and loudly cries that he will spoil the earth, and shake the whole race of men, and change them from their former good order. But hear the same prophecy speak about him again, how he thought about himself and how he bragged:

"How has Lucifer that rose at morn fallen from heaven: He is crushed to earth that sent to all the nations. But thou saidst in thy heart, 'I will go up to heaven, I will set my throne above the stars of heaven. ... I will ascend above the clouds, I will be like the Most High.' But now thou shalt go down to hell, and to the foundations of the earth."

Truly Scripture shews many things at once in this, the madness of the said spirit, his fall from the better to the worse, and the end of his fall. And having uttered terrible threats against all mankind, he discovered that men could be caught otherwise by his weapons, since they possessed in their power of free choice the ever-ready possibility of falling into evil from their own thoughts. Then he turned the conditions of states from the better to the worse, and drew away the souls of the multitude by the bait of pleasure to every form of wickedness, and left no sort of device untried, and with base myths of the gods and impure stories he tempted his victims with what they loved and with what gave them pleasure, using the artful deceit of the daemons. And in this way he took the whole world and held it captive, and obliterated the boundaries of the nations, as he had threatened to do when he said: "I will remove the boundaries of the nations, and I will diminish their strength, and I will take the whole world in my hand as a nest." And from that day forward he ruled all men with deceit, and the evil demons were arrayed under their king in every place and city and land. And thus the whole of human life was enslaved by earthly powers and evil spirits instead of the earlier ministers of God, and all gave themselves over in throngs and swiftly to the snares of pleasure; so that they soon overleapt the bounds even of nature, in unnatural offences of one kind or another, and they not only did things of which it is wrong even to think, but connected them with their conceptions of their own gods, and worked their lust with all the more freedom as a thing supposed to please the gods. Hence soon, according to the holy Apostle, they took no heed of the works of God still bright in heaven.

" They became vain in their reasonings: and their senseless heart was darkened. 22. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. 23. And changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things."

And that in the earliest age those upon earth worshipped only the lights of heaven, and knew no image, nor were concerned with the error of the daemons, there is satisfactory proof to be found in the evidence of those, who are strangers to my argument, which I drew upon in the first book of the Preparatio (which I wrote) before the present treatise; they clearly prove that the earliest men did not serve idols fashioned by hand from lifeless matter, nor even invisible daemons, but only those beings, which are said in Holy Scripture to have been distributed among the nations. It is time for the Greeks themselves, therefore, whose statements I have arranged in the work mentioned, to agree that the superstition connected with idols was something more recent and novel, being introduced subsequently to the worship of the ancients, as well as the devotion to unseen spirits. All this was the work of the said antagonist of God, who plotted against all those on earth. And all the tribe of unclean spirits co-operated with him. Yea, he surely, the prince of evil himself, worked this result, fulfilling in very deed, in the madness of strange pride, the threats he had uttered against all men, raising the godless cry, "I will be like the Most High," and with the aid of impure and evil daemons offering oracles and cures and such like in response to human sorcery.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 9

And by the prophet, "the enemy said, I will pursue and overtake," and again by another, "I will grasp the whole world in my hand as a nest, and take it up as eggs that have been left." Such, in a word, are their boasts and professions that they may deceive the godly. But not even then ought we, the faithful, to fear his appearance or give heed to his words. For he is a liar and speaks of truth never a word. And though speaking words so many and so great in his boldness, without doubt, like a dragon he was drawn with a hook by the Savior, and as a beast of burden he received the halter round his nostrils, and as a runaway his nostrils were bound with a ring, and his lips bored with an armlet. And he was bound by the Lord as a sparrow, that we should mock him. LIFE OF ST.

All sins must be avoided, to be sure, because all sins are contrary to God, but they vary in degree. The proud, for example, are God's enemies. "God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble." The devil is the prince of the proud. "Lest he be puffed up with pride," says holy Scripture, "and incur the condemnation passed on the devil," for everyone who glorifies himself in his heart is partner to the devil, who used to say, "By my own power I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I am shrewd. I have moved the boundaries of peoples." … All other failings deserve the mercy of the Lord because, in humility, they are submitted to the tribunal of God; pride alone, because it honors itself beyond its power, resists God. The adulterer or the fornicator does not dare to raise his eyes to heaven; in defection of soul, he looks for God's mercy; yet this one whom conscience bows down and humbles to the ground, it also elevates to heaven. When pride and inordinate desire for glory raise up a person, they at the same time abase him, for by his sin they make him an enemy of God.
HOMILIES ON THE PSALMS, ALTERNATE SERIES, PSALM 93

For he has said. Here he sets out the occasion of his glory from the great things which he had done, and first, as to the condition of the doer; second, as to the greatness of the deed: and I have removed; third, as to the ease of doing: and my hand has found (Isa 10:14). He shows the condition of the doer as to the power of wars: by the strength of my own hand, as to the wisdom of counselors, and by my own wisdom: but for the wrath of the enemies I have deferred it: lest perhaps their enemies might be proud, and should say: our mighty hand, and not the Lord, has done all these things (Deut 32:27).

The greatness of the deed is measured from three things: from the multitude of kingdoms; hence he says, and I have removed the bounds of the people: he speaks like someone who acquires many fields and removes the bounds by which the separate possessions were divided; as to the plundering of princes: and have taken the spoils of the princes; as to the subjugation of kings: and as a mighty man has pulled down them that sat on high, namely, on the seat of the king: whom he would, he set up: and whom he would, he brought down (Dan 5:19).

And yet in old time he had said: "I will hold the whole world in my hand as a nest, and will take it as eggs that are left: and there is no one that shall escape from me, or speak against me." He missed, then, the truth, and fell from his hope, proud and audacious though he was, and vaunting himself over the infirmity of mankind. For the Lord of powers marshalled against him the ministers of the sacred proclamations. And this verily had been foretold by one of the holy prophets when speaking of Satan and the holy teachers: "That suddenly they shall arise that bite thee: and they shall awake that afflict thee, and thou shalt be their prey." For, so to speak, they bit Satan by attacking his glory, and making his goods a spoil, and bringing them unto Christ by means of faith in Him: for so they attacked Satan himself.
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

Behold, then, how the Maker of the universe has always shown a loving care for humanity, not merely for the race of the descendants of Abraham but for all the descendants of Adam; through one tribe he has led all tribes to a knowledge of himself. He used them for this purpose both when they were religious and when they were paying the penalty for their sins. For instance, Nebuchadnezzar, the arrogant tyrant, who raised up the golden image and called on all to adore it, said, "I will gather in my hand the whole earth as a nest, as eggs that lie abandoned will I gather it."

"My hand found the strength of the people like a nest. And like abandoned eggs are collected, so I gathered all the earth. No one moved a wing, or opened a mouth, or chirped." "You sent your Spirit and the sea covered them; they descended to the depths like lead in the mighty water." When the Spirit of the Lord was sent, the Egyptians were immersed in the waters of the sea. Although we desire to see ourselves there in the word of the Lord, which is also fulfilled in us, we would do better to apply this passage to the Gentiles, who were filled with the knowledge of the truth when they received the Spirit of God. To this the prophet bore witness: "All the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, like the waters covering the sea.""They descended to the depths like lead in the mighty water." The "depths" are to be understood as carnal living, which tosses them to and fro on waves of sin. It drowns their self-absorbed souls and sends them to the bottom. Gossip, jealousy, depravity, cruelty and envy are the waves of worldly vice.
COMMENTARY ON THE CANTICLE OF EXODUS 1:10-11

The ease of doing is determined as to three things: as to absolute subjection: and my hand has found the strength of the people as a nest, which is in the power of the finder, below: and it shall come to pass, that as a bird fleeing away, and as young ones flying out of the nest (Isa 16:2); as to easy destruction: and as eggs are gathered, that are left, so have I gathered all the earth, it was so easy: but he will gather together unto him all nations, and heap together unto him all people (Hab 2:5); as to the removal of all contradiction: and there was none that moved the wing, that is, the hand—for a bird defends itself with its wing—or opened the mouth, to contradict, or whimpered, which is how wolves or birds lament: son of man, behold I take from you the desire of your eyes with a stroke, and you shall not lament, nor weep; neither shall your tears run down (Ezek 24:16).

Let us consider therefore those to whom God has granted power, to see if we may deserve to serve them and to cling to their doctrine, putting aside all pride and resisting with great courage the sin, which fearlessly operates in bodies; for death has been swallowed up by victory. On the other hand, how weak we are in this age, knowing that the church is to stand and to be led toward what is good.… You know that the ax does not boast without the man who uses it to cut … but we must fight to be able to have peace with those who keep the commandments of God.

Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it, or shall the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn? As if a rod should lift itself against him who lifts it, and a staff should exalt itself, which is but wood. Against Sennacherib, or, as many think, Nebuchadnezzar, boasting and saying: By the strength of my hand I have done it, by my wisdom I have understood, and the rest, the holy Prophet answered: O most foolish of mortals, do you think the wrath of God to be your own wisdom, and do you ascribe his command to your own strength? It is as if an axe should boast against him who holds the axe, and a saw against him by whom it is drawn, and they should say that all the works done by axe and saw were accomplished by their own skill. And if someone should lift a rod, and raise a staff to strike whom he will, and the rod and the staff themselves should boast and say that he who was struck was struck by them: so you too, though you have been the instrument of God's will, are lifted up into pride, and boast that all that is done belongs to your own power. Whatever is said to the Assyrian can also be referred both to the pride of the heretics and to the devil, who is called in the Scriptures axe and saw and rod, because through him unfruitful trees are cut down and cleft, and the hardness of unbelievers is sawn, and those who do not receive discipline are struck with the rod. The heretics too are those whose mouth is set against heaven, and their tongue passes through the earth, and who abuse the sense which they received from God for good, turning it to the contrary and the perverse, so as to speak against him by whom they were made, and to turn into blasphemy the ministry of the tongue, by which the Lord should be praised (Ps 72 [73]).

Shall the axe boast itself? Here the rebuke of the boaster is set out, because he is like an instrument, which cannot work except by the movement of the craftsman: the axe, for killing the wicked; shall the saw, for separating the good from wicked, exalt itself; a rod, for correcting; a staff, for supporting those corrected: why doth your spirit swell against God, to utter such words out of your mouth? (Job 15:13).

Therefore the Sovereign Lord of hosts will send leanness among his fat ones, and beneath his glory a burning shall be kindled and burn like the burning of fire. And the light of Israel shall be in fire, and his Holy One in flame: and his thorn and his briers shall be kindled and devoured in one day. And the glory of his forest and of his Carmel shall be consumed from the soul even to the flesh, and he shall be a fugitive for terror, and the remnants of the wood of his forest shall be numbered for their fewness, and a child shall write them down. Because you have done these things, and spoken what I related above, therefore the Lord will send his Angel, and in one night a hundred and eighty-five thousand of your army will die: so that all the most powerful, whom he calls fat, are reduced to leanness and to nothing; and, as the Hebrews relate, while the garments of the Assyrians were unharmed, their bodies were burned with a hidden fire: then the light of Israel and his holy one, that is, the angel, will be in fire and in flame, and all the thorns and briers of the Assyrians, that is, their malice, will be consumed, not over a long time, but in one day and moment. And as a forest and Carmel, which is a mountain in Galilee planted with woods, is quickly burned up when fire is set beneath it, so from the soul even to the flesh all the glory of the Assyrian will be consumed. Then the despoiled army will flee, as the same Prophet attests in what follows, and of so innumerable a multitude, which was compared to Carmel and a forest, it will come to such fewness that a little child could number them and write them down. For the Hebrews relate that only ten of his army remained; some of ours will have it that this king is a type of the adverse power. And as in Daniel (ch. 10) we read of the princes of the kingdom of the Persians, and of the kingdom of the Medes, and of the kingdom of the Greeks, so there is also a prince of the Assyrians, who because of his pride is called the great mind, and in the day of judgment will be handed over to the burnings of Gehenna, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. And that the light of Israel and the holy one, that is, the Lord himself, kindles the briers and thorns of the Assyrian, and that all his power and his innumerable peoples are to be brought to nothing. That then he, terrified with fear, like a crooked and fleeing serpent, wishes to escape the punishments hanging over him. And that those who have been able to escape from his forest and confusion and from the wood doomed to perish are worthy to be numbered and written down by the child whose government is upon his shoulders. This same thing can also be referred to the heretics: that after the Church's teaching has shone forth, and all their snares have been laid open, then they come to such desolation that, of the forest and the unfruitful trees and their innumerable multitude, which they had deceived by heretical fraud, scarcely a few remain to follow their error. Where we have rendered, the Lord will send leanness among his fat ones, the Seventy translated, the Lord will send dishonor upon your honor. And where we said: and his Holy One in flame, they rendered: and he will sanctify him in fire: by which some would have it understood that punishments and torments are applied to sinners for this purpose, that they may be purged by divine fire. And where we said: And the glory of his forest and of his Carmel, they translated: The mountains and the hills and the forests shall be quenched, whereby all the brightness and pride and multitude of the Assyrians is quenched and humbled.

Therefore the sovereign Lord, the Lord of hosts, shall send leanness. Here he threatens punishment. And concerning this, he does three things: first, he threatens the judgment of punishment; second, he determines the manner of punishment: and under his glory; third, the effect of punishment: and he shall run away through fear (Isa 10:18). Among his fat ones, the powerful and the rich, below: and the Lord of hosts shall make unto all people in this mountain, a feast of fat things (Isa 25:6).

And under. Here the manner of punishment is determined, which was through burning; and three things are set out. First, the species of punishment: his glory, that is, the multitude of his host; under, that is, under his clothes, for bodies were cremated in intact clothing, above: and your strength shall be as the ashes of tow, and your work as a spark (Isa 1:31).

And Isaiah shows that the Holy Spirit is not only light but also fire, saying, "And the light of Israel shall be for a fire." So the prophets called him a burning fire, because in those three points we see more intensely the majesty of the Godhead; since to sanctify is of the Godhead, to illuminate is the property of fire and light, and the Godhead is customarily pointed out or seen in the appearance of fire: "For our God is a consuming fire," as Moses said.

Second, the one bringing the punishment, the Holy One of Israel, God, or the angel Michael, to whom that people was committed: behold Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me (Dan 10:13); as a fire, for he will punish them through fire: all the land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy: for he shall make even a speedy destruction of all them that dwell in the land (Zeph 1:18).

Third, the one suffering the punishment, both as to the lowly, his thorns and his briers, which do not grow much; and the glory of his forest, of Lebanon, as to the great, whom he compares to high trees of Lebanon because of their dignity; from the soul even to the flesh, for they died both in soul and in body, above: for wickedness is kindled as a fire, it shall devour the brier and the thorn: and shall kindle in the thicket of the forest, and it shall be wrapped up in smoke ascending on high (Isa 9:18).

Note on the words, and the light of Israel shall be as a fire (Isa 10:17): that our God is called a fire, first, because he is subtle; and as to this, he is called subtle as to substance, because he is called spirit: God is a spirit (John 4:24); second, as to knowledge, because he is piercing: for the word of God is living and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword (Heb 4:12); third, as to appearance, because he is invisible: whence then comes wisdom? (Job 28:20); and below this: it is hid from the eyes of all living (Job 28:21), or: all men (Job 36:25). Second, because he is full of light: but that he is full of light is evident first, because he manifests as to the intellect: in your light we shall see light (Ps 35:10[36:9]); second, because he delights as to the affections: what manner of joy shall be to me, who sit in darkness and see not the light of heaven? (Tob 5:12); third, because he directs as to action, below: the Gentiles shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising (Isa 60:3). Third, because he is hot: and this is so, first, because he vivifies: you perhaps will warm them in the dust? (Job 39:14); from above he has sent fire into my bones, and has chastised me (Lam 1:13); second, because he cleanses: the vapor of the fire wastes his flesh, and he fights with the heat of the furnace (Sir 38:39); third, because he devastates: a fire is kindled in my wrath, and shall burn even to the lowest hell (Deut 32:22). Fourth, because he is light: and this is so, first, because of his motion, for the Lord has made all things for himself (Prov 16:4); second, because of his position, for he dwells on high (Ps 112[113]:5); third, because of his unmixed manner: wisdom reaches everywhere, by reason of her purity. For she is a vapor of the power of God (Wis 7:24–25).

"18. In that day the mountains shall be consumed, and the hills, and forests, and shall be devoured from soul to body. And he that flees shall be as one that fleeth from burning flame, 19. and they that are left of them shall be a number, and a little child shall write them. 20. And it shall come to pass in that day, the remnant of Israel shall no more be added, and they that are saved of Jacob shall no more trust in those that wronged them, and they shall trust in the God the holy one of Israel in truth, 21. and the remnant of Israel shall turn to the mighty God. 22. And though the people of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant of them shall be saved. 23. For he will finish the account, and cut it short in righteousness, for God will make a short account in the whole world."

And notice here, that in his denunciations of gloom, he says :

"He that fleeth shall be as one that fleeth from a burning flame; and their remnant shall be a number, and a little child shall write them"—

by which, he emphasizes the scanty number of those of the Circumcision who will escape destruction, and the burning of Jerusalem. "And they who are left," he says, "will be a number": that is they will be amenable to number, or few and easily numbered. As many, then, as those who believed in our Lord and Saviour were in comparison of the whole Jewish race, who also were thought worthy of being enrolled by Him, as the verse shews, which says: "And a little child shall write them." Having told us before Who the little child was, where he said: "Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son." And: "Before the child shall know to call on its father or mother."

And since in this place he says: "A little child shall write them," it can be seen why he said in the previous one : "And these shall be a remnant in Sion, and a remnant in Jerusalem, all shall be called holy, and shall be written in [the book of] life." As therefore among them a remnant is named, and it is they who were written in [the book of] life, so also here "the remnant from them shall be a number, and a little child shall write them." And this "remnant from Israel, and they that are saved from Jacob no more" he says "shall be with those that do them wrong, but shall trust in the Lord, the Holy One of Israel." So note if it is not with this very trust that they who went forth from the Jewish race, those who were left behind in the falling away of Israel, the disciples and apostles of our Saviour, taking no notice of the rulers of this world, or of the rulers of the people of the Circumcision who did them wrong of old, went forth to all the nations, preaching the word of Christ, and by their trust in God (for according to the prophecy "they were trusting in God, the holy one of Israel, in truth," for they gave up their whole selves in hope, without deceit or hypocrisy, but with truth) not only went forth from their own land, but prospered in that whereto they were sent. And this same remnant was like the seed of the falling away of Jacob that trusted in the strength of God, and this remnant of the whole race that once was as the sand of the sea, but not as the stars of the heaven, was thought worthy of salvation by God, as the Apostle bore witness saying :

"Isaiah cries concerning Israel, If the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved."

For of the promises gives by the oracle to Abraham concerning those who were to come after him that "they shall be as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand of the sea," the friends of God are meant, on the one hand shining like the heavenly lights, such as were those of old, the prophets and our Saviour's apostles, to whom He bore witness saying : "Ye are the light of the world" ; but, on the other, the earth-born who lie upon the ground are compared to the sand of the shore. The prophetic word speaks rightly in the above, first where the whole multitude of Israel's sons, fallen from their true and magnificent virtue to the ground, is compared to the sand of the sea, and then when it says only the remnant shall be saved. But I have now dealt sufficiently with the question of the remnant. And he says that this will come to pass, when "the Lord cutting short and completing his word shall accomplish it through the whole world" : clearly pointing to the Gospel preaching, by which, the whole Mosaic circle of symbols and signs and bodily ordinances being taken away, the complete word of the Gospel given to all men has confirmed the truth of the prophecy.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3
And he shall run away through fear. Here the effect of the punishment is set out. And first, the effect on the enemy as to their flight: and he shall run away through fear.

As to their small number, and they that remain of the trees, for Sennacherib literally fled with few, namely, with ten: you shall remain few in number, who before were as the stars of heaven for multitude (Deut 28:62).

And it shall be in that day, the remnant of Israel, and those who have been saved of the house of Jacob, shall no more lean upon him who strikes them, but shall lean upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. The remnants shall be converted, the remnants, I say, of Jacob, to the mighty Lord. For if your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of it shall be converted. The consummation cut short shall overflow with righteousness. For the Lord God of hosts will make a consummation and a cutting short in the midst of all the earth. Where in the Greek it says: The remnants of Jacob shall be converted to the mighty God, for mighty God there is written in the Hebrew EL GIBBOR (אל גבור), two names of the six names by which, as we read above, the little child and son who is given to us was called. And where it is written: The remnants shall be converted, in place of that it is said in the Hebrew in the singular number, what is left shall be converted, that is, τὸ ὑπόλειμμα ἐπιστρέψει; in the Hebrew it is written SAR JASUB (שאר ישוב). And from the occasion of this expression they think that Jasub son of Isaiah went before as a sign of the people that was to be saved out of Israel. So when the light of Israel and the holy one has consumed the forests and briers of Carmel, and the Assyrian king has fled with a few, then the remnant of Israel, who with Hezekiah as their prince, when the other cities of Judea had been taken, were besieged in Jerusalem, will in no way trust in the Assyrian, as they do now under king Ahaz, who sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians, saying: I am your servant; come up and free me from the hand of the king of Syria, and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen up against me (2 Kgs 16:7); when he took the gold and silver that was found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in the king's house, and sent gifts to the king of the Assyrians, and the Assyrian king hearkened to him, and came to Damascus, and took it, and carried it away, and killed Rezin; but, freed from that very Assyrian, the smiter, who had first been a friend and afterwards proved an enemy, they will lean and rely upon the Lord the Holy One of Israel, not falsely, as they had done under the former kings, but in truth. This we read was done under Hezekiah, so that, forsaking their idols, they were converted to the worship of God.

Second, the effect on the people: and it shall come to pass, as to three things in which they offended, namely, in their trust in the nations: upon him that strikes them, because even those from whom they sought help sometimes afflicted them, they that shall escape, either to Ezechias or to other nations: they leaned upon you (Ezek 29:7).

This is therefore what the patriarch Isaac said: You will serve your brother. But when you have removed and freed yourself from his yoke on your neck, he is signifying two future peoples, one the son of a handmaid, the other of a free woman (for the letter is a servant, but grace is free), and that people who adheres to the letter will be a servant as long as they follow the interpreter of spiritual doctrine. Then also what the Apostle said will come to pass: That the remnants may be saved according to the choice of grace. Serve your brother, therefore: but then you will feel the benefit of servitude when you begin to obey your brother willingly, rather than forcibly.
On Jacob and the Blessed Life, 3.13

And what does Isaiah cry? "Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved." Do you see that he too does not say that all are to be saved, but that those that are worthy shall? For I regard not the multitude, he means, nor does a race diffused so far distress me, but those only do I save that yield themselves worthy of it. And he does not mention the "sand of the sea" without a reason, but to remind them of the ancient promise whereof they had made themselves unworthy. Why then are you troubled, as though the promise had failed, when all the Prophets show that it is not all that are to be saved? Then he mentions the mode of the salvation also. Observe the accuracy of the Prophet, and the judgment of the Apostle, what a testimony he has cited, how exceedingly apposite! For it not only shows us that those to be saved are some and not all, but also adds the way they are to be saved. How then are they to be saved, and how will God count them worthy of the benefit? "He will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness," he says, "because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth." What he means then is somewhat of this sort. There is no need of fetching a circuit, and of trouble, and the vexation of the works of the Law, for the salvation is by a very short way. For such is faith, it holds salvation in a few short words.

But yet grace from above sometimes looks upon these mighty men, and afflicts them by the very employments caused by their abundant goods, and intersperses with their prosperity, adverse, but profitable, tribulations: in order that, when sorrowful, they may turn to their heart, and learn how vainly they are engaged in perishable pursuits. Because the light of truth, which is concealed from proud and overbusied minds, is revealed to the afflicted and humbled. For light approaches, when the afflicted mind discerns the gloom of tribulation which it is enduring from perishable pursuits: for, if it had not some perception of the light within, it would not even see that it had lost the light. But this can be specially understood also of the Jews, who dared for this reason to speak against our Redeemer, coming in the flesh, because they were mighty in their own thoughts. But the light was hid from these mighty men; because, while they are persecuting in their pride the light of truth, they lost it. But because they are to be admitted to the faith at the end of the world, it is rightly subjoined, And ordereth it to return again. Whence also it is said by Isaiah, If the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved. For the light then returns to them when they themselves return to confess the power of our Redeemer.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book XXVII, Sections 25-26

Second, as to their worship of idols, both as to manner, for in truth, the remnant, against what is said in 1 Kings 18:21: how long do you halt between two sides? If the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him; and as to the converted, the remnant of Jacob, who were left by the Assyrians: save, O Lord, your people, the remnant of Israel (Jer 31:7).

Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will?  Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?  Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?  What if God, willing to show his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:  And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory,  Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles?  As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved.  And it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people; there shall they be called the children of the living God.  Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved:  For he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth. [Isaiah 10:22-23] And as Esaias said before, Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha.  What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith.  But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness.  Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone;  As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.

How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. And this is true, because those who submit themselves to the Law are never found not to have been received. If, therefore, these things are so, it seems needless that the prophet admonished about what, once handed down, has always been observed. And could anyone so dull be found as to say that the prophet spoke something unnecessary and empty? I do not know for whom it would be safe even to hear this and not oppose it. For since the Jewish people, on account of the sins which they committed against God, seeking help from idols, were often rebuked by the prophets but refused to enter upon the path of repentance so as to return to God, God, in reproach of them, indicated that He would open His house to all nations to pray, so that, the Jews being cast off, He would show that He would place others in their place. For if the nations have always been admitted to the Law, as was said above, how could the prophet say that this would happen in the future, unless he meant something different from what had been previously commanded? He could not speak of a thing which was done daily as though it were going to come. Therefore it is clear that this tends to the ruin of the Jews, to whom the prophet shows that, with them removed, others were to be called and were to receive the house of God’s grace, which had been promised to the Jews. What that promise is, the prophet Isaiah teaches, saying: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them” (Isa. 59:20–21). Therefore this covenant is the removal of sins. This is the New Covenant, which was promised through Jeremiah, who says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I arranged for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:31–32). This is their transgression, when they made the image of a calf; then they corrupted His covenant. Therefore also the tablets on which the Law had been given were shattered under the mountain (Exod. 32:4, 19), because they deserved to receive more severe precepts. But because God is mild and merciful, He promised through the prophets that He would change the Law, so as to give another Covenant, which would differ from that which He had given before: that not only what was burdensome might be changed, but also those things which were given in figure, that is, the sabbath and circumcision; so that, since they had long been oppressed, being relieved in all things, they might give grateful thanks to God as petitioners. And because, persisting in their fathers’ transgression, they refused to turn their minds away from idols, He testifies that the nations, together with the remnant who kept the faith, will enjoy the Covenant which He had said would come: so that the faithless Jews might be tortured in a twofold way. For they were burdened for a time by the precepts, and in the future they will pay fitting penalties, because they were found faithful neither in the Old nor in the New Covenant. So He said that He would give a New Covenant, so that the Old, which had been given to the Fathers, would cease. And therefore, whoever serves God in this Covenant does not observe the sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions of foods; but has only the fear of God in faith: because he will not be justified by the Law, but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk says: “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4); so that he no longer uses many precepts to gain favor with God, but few. Isaiah again, speaking with the same meaning, says: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them shall be saved. For the Lord shall accomplish and cut short His word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short word upon the whole earth” (Isa. 10:22–23). For the remnant who will persevere in the faith of the promise, while the others do not believe, He shows the shortened word of the Law: this is the New Covenant which He promised. It would not otherwise be called a Covenant, unless in a similar way this too were confirmed by the witness of blood, just as the Old Covenant, so that both might have one and the same name: but in the Old, many precepts, in the New, however, few, as He promised. So that, since He had said that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), in the same way the sons might be justified as the father had been justified: so that, once those things ceased which began after the faith of Abraham, those who receive the faith by which that same Abraham was justified might be sons of Abraham, as was said by the Lord. And this is neither strange nor unheard of, that men should be justified without care for the sabbath and circumcision and the rest of the commandments of this sort. For Enoch did not please God by this, that he might be translated; nor was Noah found righteous in the flood by observing this alone; nor was Abraham himself justified after he was circumcised: “Abraham,” it says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8; Rom. 4:3). Then he was circumcised, so that there might be in him a sign that, though he was old, he believed that he would have a son. Therefore it is not circumcision that commends Abraham, but faith. And so, for those who believe, faith is sufficient for justification, that they may be sons of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision, because they have no need of circumcision. For what Abraham believed is not what is believed in their case. But the Jews were therefore ordered to be circumcised, so that they might have the sign of Abraham’s faith, not of their own faith, but so that they might be known as his sons according to the flesh. Yet if they believe, they will be his sons also in justification. For what advantage is it to be called the son of a powerful man if one is powerless, except that it is even more harmful? For it is a disgrace to be the son of a noble and glorious man without honor. Indeed, bodily circumcision is so far from being a merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that He will take vengeance on all the circumcised in foreskin, if they are not circumcised in heart (Jer. 4:4). Yet He is not angry with those who are circumcised in heart but uncircumcised in flesh, because no one has ever pleased God without the circumcision of the heart. Whoever, therefore, are circumcised in the flesh signify the lineage of Abraham according to the flesh; but those who are circumcised in heart signify the lineage of God according to faith, because, being circumcised from all worldly error, they confess God as their Father. What then does the circumcision of the flesh profit, if, when faith is lacking in the Jew, he cannot attain to the merit of Abraham? Or what harm is there in foreskin, when no one attains to his righteousness except the one who has followed the faith of Abraham? They therefore glory in the circumcision of the flesh in vain, since they see that it has no merit before God. And since, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, the Gentiles are better than the Jews; for the Gentiles have faith, the Jews have circumcision. And whom do you think He recognizes more as sons of Abraham: those who are like him according to the flesh, or those who are like him in faith? But the faith of Abraham bears witness. And therefore he glories not in the flesh but in faith. For this reason he has received as sons those whom he sees to be imitators of his glory. For how can he call those sons from whom he sees a shrinking back from that by which he pleased God and was justified? He will therefore be able to judge them not as his sons, but as his enemies. For they appear to be envious of him, despising the faith through which he was glorified. Nor is it surprising if the Jews are found untrusting, not at all accepting the New Testament, when we know that they were not faithful even in the Old. They were always rebellious and disrespectful against God, and therefore they received such commandments by which their necks, which were unbending, might be pressed down. For they never wished to hope for good things from God, whose such great benefits and such wondrous powers they had come to know. Therefore it is that, among other things, the prophet Ezekiel says: “I lifted up my hand to them in the desert, that they should be scattered among the nations and dispersed in the lands, because they did not perform my ordinances and rejected my commandments.” And in what follows: “I gave them laws that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live in them” (Ezek. 20:23–25). He shows for what reason such great and so harsh commandments were given to them: because they proved ungrateful for such great benefits, and, justice dictating, they were to be pressed by more severe precepts. Therefore He called them “not good,” although they are just: because they did not lead them to justification, but to destruction; and although a punishment rightly inflicted, yet for the one who suffers it, it is not a good. After these things, however, because God is merciful, He promised that He would give the New Testament, in which the shortening of the Law would justify believers, just as Abraham was justified: so that, with new moons and the sabbath and circumcision and the other precepts ceasing, not those that belong to the natural law, that is, murder, adultery, and such things, they might be justified as Abraham was. For, with the faith of Abraham renewed, He willed that all things should cease, so that the time might be such as it was when Abraham believed. But perhaps the Jews say: “If those things that were given by Moses are said to cease through the shortening of the Law, was circumcision given by Moses so that it should cease? And therefore we have the sign of our father, because we are the sons of Abraham, a sign which, for the sake of the testimony of our lineage, ought not to cease.” Circumcision indeed had to be observed in its time, that is, before the New Testament which had been promised was given. But when, by the grace of God, the burdens of the Law were ordered to cease, what need is there of circumcision? Therefore a new Law was given, that is, a spiritual one, so that carnal things might cease, and those who received it might accept its sign: so that just as in the Old Testament they had the sign of Abraham, from whom the Old Testament began, so also in the New they might have the sign of the Savior, who is the institutor of the New Testament. For just as from Abraham they were called Hebrews, so from Christ they are called Christians. Whoever, therefore, are still called Hebrews have not received the New Testament which God promised, bringing to nothing the kindness and mercy of God: for He no longer wished His people to be designated by the name of a man, but agreed to establish them under the name of His Son. With what courage, then, do the Jews say that we do not use our Law but theirs, when David says, “I will give thanks to you among the nations” (Ps. 17:50), and again, “Rejoice, O nations, with his people”?
