And I will visit upon the evils of the world, and against the ungodly their iniquities. When God visits and strikes, he strikes for this purpose, that he may amend. Accordingly, when he is vehemently angry with those who do not do penance: I will not visit, he says, upon your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor upon your daughters-in-law when they have committed adultery (Hos 4:14). On the contrary, of those who are to believe in Christ it is said (Ps 88 [89]:33): I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges: but my mercy I will not take away from them.

And I will make the pride of the unbelievers to rest, and I will humble the arrogance of the mighty. LXX: And I will destroy the insolence of the wicked, and I will humble the insolence of the proud. The Hebrew word GAON (גאון), which plainly sounds arrogance and pride, Theodotion and the Seventy always translated insolence, expressing the sense rather than the word, because every proud man is ready for insolence. Therefore the Lord visits upon the evils of the world, and against the ungodly their iniquities, for this reason: that he may curb the arrogance of the proud and humble the pride of the mighty. For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5). And in Proverbs we read: Before ruin the heart of a man is lifted up, and before glory it is humbled (Prov 16:18). Ruin always follows pride, and glory humility: For he who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14). We read in another place: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject (1 Cor 1:19). Not that true wisdom and true prudence are destroyed by the Lord, but the knowledge falsely so called: those who treasure up for themselves a lying tongue, and fail searching with searching, and find nothing, speaking iniquity on high and setting their mouth against heaven. Hence the pride of heretics is properly called insolence against the truth.

Second, he sets out equity, ordaining the punishment for the fault which they committed against themselves: I will visit, I will avenge, the evils of the world, that is, of Babylon, for it was in that monarchy, or because of the multitude of those assembling from all over; and, as to the fault which they also committed against their subjects, through the oppression of the wicked: and against the wicked; or the voiding of covenants: infidels; through the vexation of the better: arrogancy, by which they presumed to subjugate everyone, above: because the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud (Isa 2:12).

A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold. The cause is plain why God visits the οἰκουμένην, that is, the evils of Babylon: so that, deserted by its inhabitants, it may be reduced to a wilderness. Now, everything that is rare is called precious; just as above, too, according to the history, we read that because of the scarcity of men seven women take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread, and be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach (Isa 4:1). And in the volume of Samuel it is contained: The word of the Lord was precious in those days (1 Sam 3:1), that is, rare. Note that in the Hebrew PHAZ (פז) is written for gold in general, and OPHIR (אופיר) for fine gold.

A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold. LXX: And those who have been left will be more honored than refined gold, and a man will be more honorable than the stone of Sophir. At the consummation of the world, when the world has been reduced to a wilderness, and the sun darkened in its rising, and the moon has not given its splendor, such signs and portents will be wrought by the Antichrist that, as iniquity increases, the love of many will grow cold, so as to deceive, if it be possible, even the elect of God (Matt 24). Then a man will be more precious than gold, which in Hebrew is called PHAZ (פז), and Aquila translated κιῤῥὸν, which is of the finest and blood-red color; and a human being than the purest fine gold, which in Hebrew is called OPHIR (אופיר), and Aquila translated σπήλωμα ὀφεὶρ, which the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated stone of Sophir. Now it is a place of India in which the best gold is produced; as we read in Genesis of the river Phison: This is it which encircles the whole land of Evila, where there is gold; and the gold of that land is the best: and there is the carbuncle and the green stone (Gen 2:11). And more precious is understood as meaning rarer. For everything that is rare is precious, as we also read in the volume of Samuel: And the word of the Lord was precious in Israel (1 Sam 3:1).
That price is most precious. On account of this Isaiah says: "A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure gold of Ophir." This he says of Christ, who made us precious.

Third, he sets out the moderation of the punishment. And he sets out four things: first, the small number of defenders: more precious, that is, more rare: the word of God was precious (1 Sam 3:1), and a man, who can defend by power, yea a man, who can defend by counsel, the finest of gold, that is, red gold, which is the best, above: they that remain of the trees of his forest shall be so few, that they shall easily be numbered (Isa 10:19).

Upon this I will trouble heaven, and the earth will be moved from its place, because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts, and because of the day of the wrath of his fury. Either take it in the sense in which we expounded above concerning the stars, and the sun, and the moon, and the world; or ὑπερβολικῶς, that because of the indignation of God both heaven is sad and the earth is moved, and all the elements too acknowledge the wrath of the Creator.

Upon this I will shake the heaven, and the earth will be moved from its place. LXX: For the heaven will rage, and the earth will be moved from its foundations. When a man has become more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold, and that has been fulfilled which is written: Do you think, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on the earth (Luke 18:8)? then both the heavens and the earth will be moved. For heaven and earth will pass away, not by their own will and by their own choice, as many suppose, believing them to be living beings; but because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts, and because of the day of his fury, who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble. Hence what is said in the Seventy, for the heaven will rage, is to be taken μετωνυμικῶς of those who dwell in heaven, just as if we were to say: the whole city cried out, and the entire town went out to meet the judge. And of the foundations of the earth we read in Proverbs too: God by wisdom founded the earth (Prov 3:19). And the Lord says to Job: Where were you when I was founding the earth (Job 38:4)? Not that the earth has foundations laid down as a mass in the deep; but the will and power of God, by which all things are held together, is to be called its foundations. For he himself founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers, and he himself hung it upon nothing (Ps 23 [24]; Job 26).

Second, the commotion of the elements: for this I will trouble the heaven: and the earth shall be moved, as to the literal sense, there could have been a storm in the air and an earthquake in the earth; or this is hyperbole for the magnitude of their evils: I beheld the earth, and lo it was void, and nothing: and the heavens, and there was no light in them (Jer 4:23).

And it will be like a fleeing fawn, and like a flock of sheep, and there will be none to gather them: they will turn each to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. Everyone who is found will be slain, and everyone who comes upon them will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered, and their wives will be ravished. When heaven and earth have been shaken, the devil, the crooked serpent, will flee, or every doctrine contrary to the truth, which is divided into teachers and disciples: the former of whom, because of their ὀξυδέρκειαν, are called in the Greek tongue Dorcades, that is, roe-deer; the followers are like brute animals, and wandering hither and thither they have none to direct them: for they have lost him of whom it is written: The steps of a man are directed by the Lord (Prov 20:24). And these, freed from their most evil teachers, will turn to their own people, and each will flee to his own land, from which they sprang: but whoever is found will be slain, or have his throat cut. And this happens not only at the consummation of the world, but to this very day in the Church: when the teachers have been overcome, the deceived flock returns to its people and to its own land; and in that it is found, it is slain, so that it ceases to be heretical, and whoever comes upon them will fall by the spiritual sword.

And it will be like a little doe fleeing, and like a sheep, and there will be none to gather them. He means the Babylonian and Chaldean people: that at the irruption of the Medes and Persians it will flee as fearfully as a little doe and a sheep at the roaring of a lion and the howling of a wolf; and it has no defender or prince whose command it may follow.

Each will turn to his own people, and every one will flee to his own land. After Babylon has been taken and the enemy army has entered through its gates, all the auxiliaries and the troops of the various nations by which the city had formerly been defended will go back to their own provinces.

Third, as to the dispersion of those who flee, citizens and warriors as much as captives, a doe, a swift animal: deliver yourself as a doe from the hand (Prov 6:5); my flocks were scattered upon the face of the earth (Ezek 34:6).

Everyone who is found will be slain: and everyone who comes upon them will fall by the sword. He who has not fled will be struck down by the blade; and he who has chosen either to resist or to come back will be of so little use to the captured city that he too will shed his own blood.

Fourth, as to the oppression of those who remain, which occurred in three things: in the killing of men: every one that shall be found, as to citizens, every one that shall come to their aid, as to foreigners, infants, as to children: with you I will break in pieces the old man and the child (Jer 51:22).

Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes: their houses will be plundered, and their wives will be violated. This is what David prophesies in the spirit: Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you your recompense, which you have paid out to us. Blessed is he who will take and dash your little ones against the rock (Ps 136 [137]:8). So great will be the devastation of the city and the savagery of the victors that not even innocent age will be spared, that all the wealth of the houses will be plundered, and the chastity of wives will be violated before their husbands' eyes.

Then their infants and little ones, who have not yet come to the full age of error, they will dash in pieces before the eyes of the teachers, and will plunder their houses and ravish their wives, depraved wisdom and perverse doctrine. Hence for fathers of this sort, whose little ones are to be slain, we ought to pray and say: Give them, O Lord. What will you give them? A barren womb and dry breasts (Hos 9:14). For they have travailed with iniquity, they have conceived sorrow, and they have brought forth unrighteousness.

Second, in the pillaging of goods: their houses shall be pillaged: our inheritance is turned to aliens: our houses to strangers (Lam 5:2); third, as to the violation of women: their wives shall be ravished: they humiliated the women in Zion (Lam 5:11).

[Daniel 5:30-31] "On that same night Belshazzar, King of the Chaldeans, was slain, and Darius the Mede succeeded to his kingdom at the age of sixty-two." Josephus writes in his tenth book of the Jewish Antiquities that when Babylon had been laid under siege by the Medes and Persians, that is, by Darius and Cyrus, Belshazzar, King of Babylon, fell into such forgetfulness of his own situation as to put on his celebrated banquet and drink from the vessels of the Temple, and even while he was besieged he found leisure for banqueting. From this circumstance the historical account could arise, that he was captured and slaughtered on the same night, while everyone was either terrified by fear of the vision and its interpretation, or else taken up with festivity and drunken banqueting. As for the fact that while Cyrus, King of the Persians, was the victor, and Darius was only King of the Medes, it was Darius who was recorded to have succeeded to the throne of Babylon, this was an arrangement occasioned by factors of age, family relationship, and the territory ruled over. By this I mean that Darius was sixty-two years old, and that, according to what we read, the kingdom of the Medes was more sizable than that of the Persians, and being Cyrus's uncle, he naturally had a prior claim, and ought to have been accounted as successor to the rule of Babylon. Therefore also in a vision of Isaiah which was recited against Babylon, after many other matters too lengthy to mention, an account is given of these things which are to take place: "Behold I Myself will rouse up against them the Medes, a people who do not seek after silver nor desire gold, but who slay the very children with their arrows and have no compassion upon women who suckle their young" (Isaiah 13:17-18). And Jeremiah says: "Sanctify nations against her, even the kings of Media, and the governors thereof and all the magistrates thereof and all the land under the power thereof" (Jeremiah 51:28). Then follow the words: "The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing-floor during the time of its treading; yet a little while, and the time of its harvesting will come" (Jeremiah 51:33). And in testimony of the fact that Babylon was captured during a banquet, Isaiah clearly exhorts her to battle when he writes: "Babylon, my beloved, has become a strange spectacle unto me: set thou the table and behold in the mirrors those who eat and drink; rise up, ye princes, and snatch up your shields!" (Isaiah 21:4-5).
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FIVE

Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who do not seek silver nor desire gold: but with arrows they kill the little ones, and on the sucklings of the womb they will have no pity, and their eye will not spare their sons. We find in Genesis (Gen 10) that Madai was the founder of the nation of the Medes, which means measure, or from the mighty one, or from the strong one. Therefore against the Babylonians, who are confused in mind, ministers of strength are stirred up by the mighty and strong God to punish, that they may render to each according to his works. For with the measure with which they have measured, it will be measured back to them. They will return into their bosom a measure shaken down and pressed together and full and running over (Matt 7, and Luke 6). They will receive neither silver nor gold, that is, neither beauty of eloquence nor sharpness of wit, in which they formerly applauded themselves; but they will afflict with punishments those handed over to them; and they will have no pity on the little ones and the sucklings of the womb, so that they may rather show pity. And would that we too might be stirred up by the Lord, and that this power might be given to us, that we should desire neither the silver nor the gold of worldly eloquence and wisdom, but should kill the sons of the heretics, and of all who have been deceived, with spiritual arrows, that is, with the testimonies of the Scriptures: and that those who are nourished with the milk of error may be slaughtered without any mercy, so that they may perish by a merciful cruelty, and that we may have pity on no infancy, and may be worthy of that beatitude: Blessed is he who will take hold of his little ones and dash them against the rock!

Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who will not seek silver, nor want gold. What lay hidden has been made plain: that the mighty ones and the giants are by no means to be understood as angels and demons, but as the nation of the Medes, whose prince Darius was the first to destroy the empire of the Babylonians, having slain Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, who was the son of Evil-merodach (Dan 5). And he describes the savagery of the Medes and Persians as so great that, in their ardor to shed blood, they despise gold and silver and count the riches offered to them as mud.
Behold I will stir up the Medes against them. Here he describes the ferocity of the enemy, which is not appeased by tribute: who shall not seek silver.

But with arrows they will kill the little ones, and they will have no pity on the sucklings of the womb, and their eye will not spare the sons. The little ones will be killed, whose wounds will be no smaller than their bodies; and the wombs of pregnant women will be cut open, and the infants dashed out, and the cruel victor will kill the sons pressed to the breasts.

Nor softened by mercy: but with their arrows they shall kill the children, neither on powerless men: the sucklings, nor on little children: their sons: behold, I will bring upon her, and she shall be utterly destroyed (Jer 51:64).

And Babylon, that glorious one among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah: it will not be inhabited unto the end, and it will not be founded unto generation and generation. We have heard of the Medes, we have heard of Babylon, we have heard of her who is renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans: and we refuse to understand what was, and seek to hear what was not. And we say this, not because we condemn the tropological understanding, but because the spiritual interpretation ought to follow the order of the history; and many, ignorant of this, wander about in the Scriptures in a frenzied error. To this present day, then, the prophecy concerning Babylon is being fulfilled: and just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, so this city too, once overthrown, will not be inhabited forever. For in its place they made Seleucia and Ctesiphon the renowned cities of the Persians.

And Babylon, that glorious one among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. It will not be inhabited to the end, and it will not be founded unto generation and generation: nor will the Arab pitch his tents there, nor will shepherds rest there: but wild beasts will rest there, and their houses will be filled with dragons: and ostriches will dwell there, and hairy ones will dance there; and owls will answer there in its dwellings, and sirens in the shrines of pleasure. Its time is near to come, and its days will not be prolonged. LXX: And Babylon, which is called renowned, the glorious one of the king of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; it will not be inhabited forever, nor will anyone enter it for many generations; nor will Arabs pass through it, nor will shepherds rest in it; but wild beasts will rest there, and the houses will be filled with noise, and sirens will lie down there, and demons will dance there, and onocentaurs will dwell there; and hedgehogs will make their dens in their houses. It will come quickly and will not delay. What follows: And its days will not be drawn out, ⁚ is to be marked with asterisks, because it was added from Theodotion. When the Medes have been stirred up against the city of confusion, who count neither gold nor silver among good things, who kill the little ones with arrows and have no pity on the sucklings of the womb, and whose eye does not spare their sons, the city once renowned, which was in the pride of the Chaldeans, who mean as demons, will be overthrown just as Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown, so that no trace of its former dwelling remains in it: but after there has been a new heaven and a new earth, and the form of this world has passed away (1 Cor 7), the city of confusion will not be inhabited forever, and will by no means recover the same state. For after it has ceased to be in its former glory, the Arab, who means western and of the evening, will not pitch his tents there, so as to desire to dwell in that which he has seen to be deserted. Now the Arab in the present passage is taken in the good sense, because he always strains toward the end and, forgetting what lies behind, stretches himself out to what lies before. Nor will the shepherds rest there, who are accustomed to feed the most gentle flock of the Lord in Jerusalem; but on the contrary, wild beasts will rest there, which the Psalmist detests, saying: Do not deliver to the beasts the soul that confesses to you (Ps 73 [74]:19). For these Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, SIIM (ציים). And their houses, that is, those of the Babylonians, will be filled, according to the Seventy and Theodotion, ἤχου, that is, with noise and clamors; according to Aquila, with typhoons, which we have turned into dragons; according to Symmachus, with OIIM (אחים), the word contained in the Hebrew. And ostriches will dwell there, an animal that always seeks out solitudes, of which more is written in Job: which, though it seems to have wings, yet is not lifted high above the earth: for which the Seventy translated σειρῆνας, that is, sirens. The hairy ones, who in Hebrew are called SIRIM (שעירים), Theodotion translated as with hair erect and standing up; Symmachus and the Seventy translated demons. For the onocentaurs too, which the Seventy alone translated, imitating the fables of the Gentiles, who say that there were hippocentaurs, the three other translators set down the Hebrew word itself, IIM (איים), which we have turned into owls. And where the Seventy said, hedgehogs will make their dens in their houses, and in the Hebrew THANNIM (תנים) is set down, Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated sirens, signifying either some kind of beasts, or demons who, according to the error of the Gentiles, sing sweetly and deceive men who cannot pass through the shipwreck of this world with stopped ears. Moreover the name onocentaur, compounded of asses and centaurs, seems to me to signify those who in part have some human understanding, and again are drawn away into vices by pleasures and the mire of baseness. It is said, therefore, according to tropology, that at the end of the world, or of each one's death, all the glory and pride of the Chaldeans and the confusion of the world will depart from us; and that all things will be overthrown as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; and that the state of this world will be no more, but will perish forever. Nor will the Arab pitch his tents there, of whom it is said in the sixty-seventh psalm: Make a way for him who rides upon the setting of the sun; the Lord is his name (Ps 67 [68]:5). Nor will the shepherds rest there, namely the angels who preside over the human race and daily see the face of the Father: but wild beasts and dragons and ostriches and hairy ones and owls and sirens will rest there, all of which beasts we understand figuratively as angels, or demons, and those to whom we are handed over for punishment. And in the houses once of pleasure, where there was gladness and joy, there will be the wailing of owls and the lamentable voice of the sirens, which leads its hearers to death. That the time of judgment is imminent, and that the day of the consummation of Babylon is not prolonged, he will by no means wonder who sees Babylon daily overthrown through holy men in those who believe in the Lord, and who sees that every length of time, compared with eternity, is near. Of the kinds of beasts, or rather of monsters, we have spoken briefly, because in the former book they were in part touched upon according to the history. This too is to be considered: that after the Church's preaching and the teaching of the Savior have overthrown the city of confusion, so that it is compared to Sodom and Gomorrah, it is not inhabited by holy men, nor do the shepherds rest in it who were accustomed to feed the flock of Christ: but on the contrary, wild beasts and dragons and ostriches rest there, and hairy ones dance in it. For whatever the heretics say in the synagogues of Satan is not the teaching of the Lord, but the howling of demons and of hairy ones, whom Esau imitated. And sirens will rest in the shrines of pleasure, who with sweet and deadly song draw souls down into the deep, so that, as the shipwreck rages, they may be devoured by wolves and dogs. Near, therefore, and pressing daily is the time of the ruin of the heretics, and their overthrow is not deferred.

And that Babylon. Here he describes Babylon's subsequent desolation. And first, the destruction of the city: turned, that is, overturned, as Sodom, about which Revelation 18:10 says: alas! Alas! That great city, Babylon, that mighty city: for in one hour is your judgment come.

Nor will the Arab pitch his tents there; nor will shepherds rest there: but beasts will be there, their houses will be filled with dragons, and ostriches will dwell there, and hairy ones will dance there. And owls will answer in its buildings, and Sirens in the shrines of pleasure. Babylon will be so devastated and deserted that it will not be useful even for the pasturing of herds and flocks. For the Arab and the Saracen will not pitch their tents there, nor will shepherds, weary with toil after the tracks of their flocks, rest there; but among the broken walls and the narrow places of the ancient ruins SIIM (ציים) will dwell: which the Seventy alone translated as beasts; the others kept the very name that is written among the Hebrews, wishing kinds of demons or phantoms to be understood. And their houses, he says, will be filled, as we have said, with dragons; as Aquila translated, with typhoons; as Symmachus, OHIM (אחים), expressing the Hebrew word itself; but the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted it as cries or sounds. And as for what follows: Hairy ones will dance there, they understand either incubi, or satyrs, or certain wild men of the woods, whom some call the fig-tree Fauns, or kinds of demons. For owls, too, all kept the Hebrew word itself, IIM (איים); the Seventy alone translated onocentaurs. And the Sirens are called THENNIM (תנים), which we shall interpret either as demons, or as certain monsters, or at any rate as great dragons, which are crested and fly. By all these things the signs of devastation and solitude are shown: that the depopulation of the once most mighty city is so great that, because of the multitude of demons and beasts, none of the shepherds, that is, of those who seek out the desert, dares to enter it. We have learned from a certain brother, an Elamite, who came out of those regions and now lives the life of the monks at Jerusalem, that there are royal hunting grounds in Babylon, and that beasts of every kind are kept enclosed merely by the circuit of its walls.

Second, as to its perpetual solitude: it shall no more be inhabited: him that bends his bow shall not live there, and him that is armed with a coat of mail shall not go up (Jer 51:3). Third, as to the horror of its solitude, which is shown by the flight of shepherds: neither shall the Arabian pitch his tents there, who do not have fixed houses, but wander through the desert, nor shall shepherds of sheep.

Wherefore I entreat, let us kill the serpent, let us shut up the wild beasts, let us stifle them, let us slay them, and these wicked thoughts let us give over to the sword of the Spirit, lest the prophet threaten us also with such things as he threatened Judea, that "The wild asses shall dance there, and porcupines, and serpents." For there are, there are even men worse than wild asses, living as it were in the wilderness, and kicking; yea the more part of the youth amongst us is like this. For indeed having wild lusts they thus leap, they kick, going about unbridled, and spend their diligence on no becoming object. And the fathers are to blame, who while they constrain the horsebreakers to discipline their horses with much attention, and suffer not the youth of the colt to go on long untamed, but put upon it both a rein, and all the rest, from the beginning; but their own young ones they overlook, going about for a long season unbridled, and without temperance; disgracing themselves, by fornications, and gamings, and continuings in the wicked theatres.
Homily 59 on the Gospel of Matthew

But it would take too long to search through the whole of Scripture and run through the different kinds of them, as they are termed by the prophets onocentaurs, satyrs, sirens, witches, howlers, ostriches, urchins; and asps and basilisks in the Psalms; and are called lions, dragons, scorpions in the gospel, and are named by the Apostle the prince of this world, rulers of this darkness, and spirits of wickedness. And all these names we ought not to take as given at random or hap-hazard, but as alluding to their fierceness and madness under the sign of those wild beasts which are more or less harmful and dangerous among us, and by comparing them to the poisonous wickedness or power which among other beasts or serpents, some pre-eminence in evil confers on them, they are called by their names, in such a way that to one is assigned the name of lion because of the fury of his rage and the madness of his anger, to another that of basilisk because of his deadly poison, which kills a person before it is perceived, and to another that of onocentaur or urchin or ostrich because of his sluggish malice.
First Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 32

As to the inhabitation of beasts and the dead: but wild beasts shall rest there, who love solitude. Dragons, who, according to some, are large winged serpents, according to others, are large fish with wet scales, and according to others, are cubit long serpents that eat other serpents and, because of this, poison with the breath of their mouths. Ostriches, animals which have wings but do not fly, indeed, they walk on their feet: the wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron (Job 39:13). The hairy ones, that is, hairy animals, like foxes, wolves, and suchlike; or wild men, hairy and shaggy, who are said by some to not be true men, but to have the shape of a man, or of a demon assuming a body in such a shape: frequenting such deserted dwellings, they go about through the night and disturb men in various ways. Owls, birds the size of a raven, spattered with spots, so called because they have a voice like the howling of wolves. Sirens, according to some, crested and winged serpents, or fish of the sea that have the likeness of a woman, or birds that sing sweetly; in the temples of pleasure, that is, places where they would luxuriate, below: and it shall be the habitation of dragons, and the pasture of ostriches, and demons and monsters and the hairy ones shall meet (Isa 34:13–14).

Its time is near to come, and its days will not be prolonged. He says that the time is at hand when it is to be taken by its enemies. For after the captivity of Jerusalem, with no long time in between, it too was laid waste by the Medes and Persians.
14: Truly his will shall be fulfilled swiftly and suddenly, as the Scripture testifies.

For the proselytes have no need of a covenant, if, since there is one and the same law imposed on all that are circumcised, the Scripture speaks about them thus: 'And the stranger shall also be joined with them, and shall be joined to the house of Jacob.'

The stranger will be joined to them, and will cleave to the house of Jacob, and peoples will take them, and bring them into their own place, and the house of Israel will possess them upon the land of the Lord as menservants and maidservants: and they will take captive those who had taken them captive, and they will subdue their taskmasters. We conjecture that many from various nations came to Jerusalem with the people of the Jews, believing in the God of Israel and abandoning the idols of their errors. And that they were brought back by the king's letters, and received gifts and the expenses of the Temple, there is no doubt. The understanding seems to be hemmed in only on this point: how Israel possessed, in the land of the Lord, those who had once been its conquerors, and subdued its taskmasters, and held them as menservants and maidservants. Unless perhaps synecdochically we understand the whole from the part: that they afterwards enjoyed such prosperity that they acquired for themselves households of menservants and maidservants from the various nations round about as well. It can also be understood of the times of Ahasuerus (Esth 9; Jdt 13), when, after Holofernes had been killed, the enemy army was cut down by Israel. That I cling to the letter and, in the manner of the serpent, eat earth, is your will, who have wished to hear only the historical interpretation.

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose out of Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil: the stranger will be joined to them, and will cleave to the house of Jacob. And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place: and the house of Israel will possess them upon the land of the Lord as menservants and maidservants; and they will take captive those who had taken them captive, and they will subdue their oppressors. And it will be in that day, when God has given you rest from your labor, and from your trouble, and from the hard bondage in which you served before: you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and you will say. For stranger, that is, proselyte, the Seventy translated γηώραν, which in Hebrew is called GER (גר). Hence I think that the son of Moses too, who was a stranger in the land, was named by his father Gersam (Exod 1). Therefore georas is a Hebrew word declined after Greek custom: although someone ignorant of the Hebrew tongue tries to express a Greek etymology in it, from the fact that it has the care of an earthly thing: for γῆ, he says, is the word for earth, and ὤρα, φροντὶς, that is, care. Again, for MASAL (משל), which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated parable, and whom we too have followed, the Seventy translated lament. Now the order is this: after Babylon has been deserted forever, so as to be a dwelling of wild beasts, the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, namely on him who supplanted vices; and he will choose Israel, him who beholds God with the mind. And note the propriety of the words: on Jacob, who is still set in the wrestling, he will have mercy; but to Israel, who received the name after the victory, not mercy but election is fitted. He will also make them rest upon their own land, of which the Savior speaks: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land (Matt 5:4), and I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps 26 [27]:13). There will also be joined to the house of Jacob those who were chosen through the Apostles, the multitude of the nations; and they will take the remnant of the house of Israel and bring them to their own place, so that they may dwell in their tents; and the house of Israel will possess them upon the land of the Lord as menservants and maidservants. For it profits the wicked to serve the good. Hence it is said to Esau too: You shall serve your brother. And to Jacob: Your brother shall serve you (Gen 27). And they will take those who had formerly deceived them with sophistries: and they will reduce to bondage their oppressors, who do all things for the sake of gain. And after Jacob and Israel have rested from their labor, in which they had labored much fighting against the world and the heretics, and from their trouble and bondage, in which they had formerly served a malignant interpretation and false doctrines, then they will take up a lament and parable against the king of Babylon, namely the discourse of heretical error and confusion, and will say what follows. The Jews interpret this passage carnally, but they will not be able to show that it came to pass after they returned from Babylon. For neither did the Babylonians, who had first taken them captive, serve them; nor, when the Babylonians were conquered, did they possess their houses; nor did they have them as menservants and maidservants. It remains, therefore, that according to their fables they think this will come about in respect of this Roman empire: that when the Romans have been overcome in the last time, the nations whom they formerly served will serve them. But if, by following the letter, they deceive themselves with a false hope, who will grant them that Rome is called Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar the king of the Roman empire?

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose from Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil. Of this Zephaniah speaks more fully: Praise, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, Israel; be glad and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem: for the Lord has taken away your judgment: he has turned away your enemies (Zeph 3:14-15). And it signifies the time when Cyrus king of the Persians permitted the captive people to return to Jerusalem. Read the book of Ezra (Ezra 1), Haggai (Hag 1) and Zechariah (Zech 1): when, under Zerubbabel, and Joshua the high priest, and Ezra, and Nehemiah, the altar, the Temple, and the walls of the city were built.

Her time is near at hand. In this part, he promises liberation to the Jews through the destruction of Babylon, which he threatened above. And this is divided into three parts: in the first, he promises liberation; in the second, he foretells the insults of the liberated against their oppressor: and it shall come to pass in that day (Isa 14:3); in the third, he sets out the confirmation of the insult: the seed of the wicked shall not be named (Isa 14:20).

Concerning the first, he sets out three things: the shortness of time: near at hand is the day of the Lord, to whom all things are present, or after our subjugation, her days, of subjugation: the day of destruction is at hand, and the time makes haste to come (Deut 32:35).

Second, he sets out the manner and order of liberation, and first, as to the relief of their misery: for the Lord will have mercy: he will turn again, and have mercy on us (Mic 7:19); as to the recovery of divine favor: and will yet choose, namely, some of them: the Lord your God has chosen you (Deut 7:6); as to the restoration of their homeland: and will make them rest: I will bring them to their own land: and I will feed them in the mountains of Israel (Ezek 34:13).

Third, he describes the dignity of the liberated, as to the adhering of strangers to them: the stranger shall be joined: draw nigh to God: and he will draw nigh to you (Jas 4:8).

As to honorable retention: the people, among whom they were taken captive, shall take them, namely, the Jews, as though to carry them in their arms, below: and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders (Isa 49:22); or otherwise, as to the leading away of those who adhered to them, the people, namely, the Jews, shall take, that is, retain, them, leading those who adhered to them with themselves; as to the subjugation of the enemy or of those who adhered to them: and the house of Israel shall possess them, as they once possessed Israel: I will return your recompense upon your own heads (Joel 3:7).

And it will come to pass in that day, when the Lord has given you rest from your labor, and from your turmoil, and from your hard servitude, because you served before: you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and you will say. The discourse is directed to Israel: that after it has returned to Jerusalem and shaken off the yoke of servitude, it should recall the former power of Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian summit, and lament him with a pitiful voice, because he has come to such calamity that he seems worthy of pity even to his enemies.

And it shall come to pass. Here the insult of the liberated people against their captor, who has now been destroyed, is set out.

And first, the title or the inscription is set out, containing three things: the time, when God shall give you rest from your labor, by which you have labored in waging war; and from your vexation, of captivity, by which you were kept in prison; and from bondage, by which you were oppressed in the land of your captivity.
We will show in what follows that these things are not said of someone else but of that tyrant, the one without shame, the enemy of God, as Isaiah says.

According to Isaiah, in which lament is offered on behalf of the king of Babylon, much can be learned about the origin and beginning of evil. Evil derived its existence from some who had lost their wings by following the one who was first to lose his own wings.

How has the taskmaster ceased, the tribute come to rest? The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers, that struck the peoples in indignation, that subdued the nations in fury with an incurable blow, that persecuted cruelly: it has come to rest and fallen silent: the whole earth has rejoiced and exulted. This is the voice of Israel lamenting and pitying: how one who was once a lord and conqueror of the lands, despoiling everything with tributes, has been crushed and brought to nothing. He, I say, who was the staff of the wicked, who as sceptre and royal rod struck all in his fury, whose blow could not be endured, who cruelly pursued even those who fled: how he has come to rest and been humbled, and at his ruin the whole earth has fallen silent, uttering only the voice of exultant joy!

How has the oppressor ceased, the tribute come to rest? The Lord has broken the staff of the ungodly, the rod of the rulers, which struck the peoples in indignation with an incurable stroke, which subdued the nations in fury, persecuting cruelly. In the Epistle of Peter we read: It is time for judgment to begin at the house of God (1 Pet 4:17). And in Ezekiel it is said to the tormentors: Begin at my holy ones (Ezek 9:6). For the order of judgment is arranged according to the diversity of sin, so that those who have offended less are purged first. And the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Therefore, when Israel has been freed from hard bondage, he will take up a parable against the king of Babylon, which we ought to understand as a parable. For if the discourse is against Nebuchadnezzar, and a simple exposition of the history, how is it called a parable, when it παραβάλλεται, that is, is compared, to nothing else? Israel therefore wonders how the oppressor has ceased, who was accustomed to exact payment down to the last farthing. And he was accustomed to exact from none but debtors, who say in the Lord's Prayer: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matt 6:12). To this exactor debtors are handed over by the judge, who sends them into prison and exacts down to the least sin. Accordingly Paul the apostle too handed over to the exactor the Corinthian fornicator, who had taken his father's wife, and also Phygellus and Hermogenes (1 Cor 5; 2 Tim 1). And of these exactors it is also said above: My people, your oppressors plunder you; and those who demand payment rule over you. For tribute Aquila translated famine. For since the bridegroom has been taken from us, we suffer a famine of the word of God and fast continually from the body of the Lord.

Because the Lord Jesus would destroy their staff, that is, their power to oppress, Isaiah said, "How has the oppressor ceased and the tax ended? Was his oppressor's staff destroyed?" It befits Christians to be cautious, therefore, and it is right for the people of the Lord to be observant, lest oppressors who had once been repelled by divine grace should rouse themselves again to demand the kind of taxes which are paid with spiritual delinquency.
COMMENTARY ON THE CANTICLE OF DEUTERONOMY 2:10

You shall take up this parable, that is, a sermon of similitudes, which says one thing and signifies another: for the things spoken of in the parable signify the condition of Nabuchodonosor, as to his power, his fault and his punishment, because of which these things could have happened, even if they did not happen: against the king of Babylon; in that day a parable shall be taken up upon you, and a song shall be sung with melody (Mic 2:4); shall not all these take up a parable against him? (Hab 2:6).

The insult itself is set out: and first, of the living; second, of the dead: hell below (Isa 14:9). The insult of the living contains three things: his destruction with the fault which he committed in exacting tributes: how is the exactor come to nothing.

And for this reason the rod and staff of the ungodly, for which the Seventy translated yoke, strikes us, or oppresses us, because we would not bear the lightest yoke, the yoke of the Savior. And with this staff and this rod he struck the nations with incurable fury, and cruelly pursued those who fled: not wishing to amend those handed over to him, but to kill them.

In inflicting punishments on men: the Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers, that struck the people in wrath, as though in reply to a preceding question; in attacking kingdoms: that brought nations under: how is the hammer of the whole earth broken, and destroyed (Jer 50:32).
That struck the people in wrath with an incurable wound, that brought nations under in fury, that persecuted in a cruel manner: how is the hammer of the whole earth broken, and destroyed (Jer 50:32).

The whole earth has come to rest and fallen silent; it has rejoiced and exulted; the fir trees too have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon. Since you have fallen asleep, no one comes up to cut us down. Hell beneath was troubled: to meet your coming it stirred up the giants for you. All the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones; all the princes of the nations, all of them will answer and say to you: You too have been wounded as we were, you have become like us? Your pride has been dragged down to hell, your corpse has fallen; beneath you the moth will be spread, decay, and worms will be your covering. At the destruction of the ungodly king, who struck the nations with an incurable stroke and pursued them cruelly, the whole earth came to rest and fell silent, which before was full of tumults and sedition, so much so that the fir trees and the cedars of Lebanon rejoiced, of which it is written in the psalms: You brought a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations and planted it. Its shade covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God (Ps 79 [80]:9). These cedars of God, because at one time they sinned, the Lord handed over to punishments to be broken. Hence in another psalm it is said: The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon (Ps 28 [29]:5). And the fir trees ought to be taken as all the lofty, those who are sublime in the service of the Lord, who said with harmonious voice: Since you have fallen asleep. Note that even the death of death is called a sleeping. No one comes up to cut us down. For when the strong man has been overcome and his vessels plundered, the rest of his attendants also have fallen. Hence the Lord too says in the Gospel (Matt 25:41): Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. How many have these fellers of timber and trees cut down with their axes and made to fall?

Second, it contains the ensuing peace: the whole earth is quiet, ceasing from that tumult, and still, ceasing from weeping, it is glad, in your destruction, and has rejoiced, in its liberation: the just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge (Ps 58:10).

The fir trees too have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon: Since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down. By the fir trees and cedars of Lebanon understand the princes of the nations, who were cut down when Nebuchadnezzar struck them; and they too, breaking out into a voice of joy, say: Since you were led down to the underworld, no one else could be found to cut down the great and the mighty.

Third, it contains the eagerness of the princes: the fir trees also, which signify those elevated in dignity; similar to this is what is found in Ezekiel 31:8: the cedars in the paradise of God were not higher than he. You have slept, with the sleep of the dead; cut us down, that is, kill us.

Hell too, troubled, or turned to bitterness, to meet the coming of the true Nebuchadnezzar, is the place of punishments and torments, in which the rich man clothed in purple is seen: to which the Lord also descended, to release the bound from prison. We can also call hell, coming to meet him, that angel who is set over the punishments of hell, who stirred up all the giants: for which some have translated Raphaim, others Titans. And they are called giants according to the custom of the heathen, who suppose them earth-born, whom the earth begot. But we, according to the etymology of the Greek word, can call giants those who have served earthly works. Then there follows: All the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones, at the coming of their former prince: so that him whom they formerly honored for his power they might afterward marvel at in punishments, and say: You too have been wounded as we also were: you have become like us. These words have this sense: We thought that we, because of our weakness, had not been able to resist the power of God, and that you alone were the one who would remain in your loftiness; but, as the facts show, you too have been wounded and taken, and have become like us; so that those whom rank separated on earth, punishment unites in hell.

The underworld beneath you was thrown into confusion, at the meeting of your coming it roused up giants for you: all the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones: all the princes of the nations, every one, will answer and say to you. These things are to be read emphatically and in the manner of a stage scene; not because they happened, but because they could have happened; unless perhaps we believe that the souls of the kings whom he had killed came to meet the Babylonian king, mocking him. For it is a solace in evils when men see their enemies suffer the same things:

Hell below. Here the insult of the dead against Nabuchodonosor is set out, and first, that of the princes and the powerful, second, of the others: they that shall see you (Isa 14:16).

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he sets out the meeting with the lower regions, as to the ministers of punishments or officials: hell, that is, the devil, who is set over hell, below, for hell is below, was in an uproar, that is, turned to tumult, as if this could happen, below (ch. 30). Likewise as to other powers rushing in: it will stir up the giants for you, as though to rise to you with them; giants, as to the strong in body, below: let not the dead live, let not the giants rise again (Isa 26:14).

All the princes of the earth, as to kings, to whom it belongs to sit in thrones; the princes of the nations, as other power; but they are risen up.

And you too have been wounded as we were, you have become like us: your pride has been dragged down to the underworld: there has fallen your corpse; beneath you the moth will be spread, and worms will be your covering. The speech of the mighty ones and princes of the earth, whom he had called cedars and fir trees above, is addressed to the Babylonian king, now placed in the underworld. We no longer grieve that we were cut down, since you too have fallen by the same axe. All your power, and your pride lifted up to heaven, has been dragged down to the earth. So will your corpse too feed the moth, and a multitude of swarming worms cover it? Through death you will feel the worthlessness of man, you who displayed the power of God in yourself.

All, namely, all the giants of hell, shall answer, as if you had summoned them, or as though crying.

Second, he sets out their reproach. And they reproach him with three things: namely, the punishment which he found, as to his death: you also are wounded, in death, by the force of divine power: you have humbled the proud one, as one that is wounded (Ps 89:10).

Your pride has been dragged down to hell, or your glory, and your corpse has fallen, or, as the Seventy translated, your great gladness, in which you formerly rejoiced when the nations were subject to you. Beneath you decay will be spread, and worms will be your covering. This is the rest of the devil, this the bed of the tempter, who was lifted up into such pride that he dared even to tempt the Lord, saying: All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matt 4:9). The decay and the moth and the covering of worms are understood either as the eternal punishments which one's own conscience begets, or as the material of torments, which is born from one's own sins. For just as, so long as there is matter in a corpse and any moisture in the corpse, worms are born from decay, so from the very matter of sins torments are begotten. Hence the Apostle Paul too, death having been slain, to which the prophetic word spoke through Hosea: I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell (Hos 13:14), says to it: Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death (1 Cor 15:55)? For when it is dead, there is no one to cut us down: for there will by no means be sin that must be cut down, since the sting of death is sin.

Then as to the humiliation of the dead man, both in soul, your pride is brought down to hell, and in body, your carcass of death is fallen down; then also as to the affliction of the dead man in hell: under you shall the moth be strewed; worms, in which all the punishments of hell are designated: he will give fire, and worms into their flesh, that they may burn, and may feel for ever (Jdt 16:21).

It is most clearly proved by these words that he who formerly was Lucifer and who "arose in the morning" has fallen from heaven. For if, as some suppose, he was a being of darkness, why is he said to have formerly been Lucifer or lightbearer? Or how could he "rise in the morning" who had in him no light at all?… So he was light once … when "his glory was turned into dust."

How can we possibly suppose that what is said in many places by Scripture, especially in Isaiah, about Nebuchadnezzar is said about a human being? For no human being is said to have "fallen from heaven" or to have been "Lucifer" or the one who "arose every morning."

SUCH was their position. While those on the side of the opposing rebel power were either daemons, or vile spirits immersed more or less in wickedness, with the cunning ruler of them all the mighty daemon, who first failed of their reverence of the Divinity and fell from their own portion, when envy of man's salvation drew them the contrary way, plotting with all sorts of evil devices against all the nations, and even against the Lord's portion in their jealousy of the good. It is this godless and unholy scheme of the great Daemon, which the prophetic spirit in Isaiah reproves in this way, saying:

"13. I will act in strength, and in the wisdom of understanding I will take away the boundaries of the nations, and will diminish their strength, 14. and I will shake inhabited cities. And the whole inhabited world I will take in my hand as a nest, and I will take them even as eggs that have been left; and none shall escape me or say me nay."

These are the words of God's antagonist, boasting in the strength of his wickedness, as he threatens to steal and obliterate the divisions of the nations delivered by the Most High to the angels, and loudly cries that he will spoil the earth, and shake the whole race of men, and change them from their former good order. But hear the same prophecy speak about him again, how he thought about himself and how he bragged:

"How has Lucifer that rose at morn fallen from heaven: He is crushed to earth that sent to all the nations. But thou saidst in thy heart, 'I will go up to heaven, I will set my throne above the stars of heaven. ... I will ascend above the clouds, I will be like the Most High.' But now thou shalt go down to hell, and to the foundations of the earth."

Truly Scripture shews many things at once in this, the madness of the said spirit, his fall from the better to the worse, and the end of his fall. And having uttered terrible threats against all mankind, he discovered that men could be caught otherwise by his weapons, since they possessed in their power of free choice the ever-ready possibility of falling into evil from their own thoughts. Then he turned the conditions of states from the better to the worse, and drew away the souls of the multitude by the bait of pleasure to every form of wickedness, and left no sort of device untried, and with base myths of the gods and impure stories he tempted his victims with what they loved and with what gave them pleasure, using the artful deceit of the daemons. And in this way he took the whole world and held it captive, and obliterated the boundaries of the nations, as he had threatened to do when he said: "I will remove the boundaries of the nations, and I will diminish their strength, and I will take the whole world in my hand as a nest." And from that day forward he ruled all men with deceit, and the evil demons were arrayed under their king in every place and city and land. And thus the whole of human life was enslaved by earthly powers and evil spirits instead of the earlier ministers of God, and all gave themselves over in throngs and swiftly to the snares of pleasure; so that they soon overleapt the bounds even of nature, in unnatural offences of one kind or another, and they not only did things of which it is wrong even to think, but connected them with their conceptions of their own gods, and worked their lust with all the more freedom as a thing supposed to please the gods. Hence soon, according to the holy Apostle, they took no heed of the works of God still bright in heaven.

" They became vain in their reasonings: and their senseless heart was darkened. 22. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. 23. And changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things."

And that in the earliest age those upon earth worshipped only the lights of heaven, and knew no image, nor were concerned with the error of the daemons, there is satisfactory proof to be found in the evidence of those, who are strangers to my argument, which I drew upon in the first book of the Preparatio (which I wrote) before the present treatise; they clearly prove that the earliest men did not serve idols fashioned by hand from lifeless matter, nor even invisible daemons, but only those beings, which are said in Holy Scripture to have been distributed among the nations. It is time for the Greeks themselves, therefore, whose statements I have arranged in the work mentioned, to agree that the superstition connected with idols was something more recent and novel, being introduced subsequently to the worship of the ancients, as well as the devotion to unseen spirits. All this was the work of the said antagonist of God, who plotted against all those on earth. And all the tribe of unclean spirits co-operated with him. Yea, he surely, the prince of evil himself, worked this result, fulfilling in very deed, in the madness of strange pride, the threats he had uttered against all men, raising the godless cry, "I will be like the Most High," and with the aid of impure and evil daemons offering oracles and cures and such like in response to human sorcery.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 9

[On why God created the world:] And lest we seem to have passed over the mystery, or rather to have been ignorant why the world was made, we say that the apostasy of the Devil drew many angels, that is, spiritual powers, with him into transgression, when he willed by wicked presumption to defend a kingdom for himself. This the prophet Isaiah signifies, saying, “How are you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning?” (Isa. 14:12); that is, you who appeared brighter than the rest. For he was a sort of prince of many, among whom he was more splendid, and with whose company he descended into wicked conflict. Seeing beneath himself many spiritual powers, since in the paradise of God he was more excellent in the knowledge of the heavenly mystery, swollen with pride itself, he wished to be called god. In this, moreover, we see in the present life that some have imitated his example: men who, puffed up by the contemplation of the troops of soldiers gathered around them, and with their attendants supplying fuel for conspiracy in this matter, have tried to claim dominion for themselves. From this it came about that God, in order to destroy his presumption not by power but by reason, created matter which would be a confusion of things, from which He would make the world.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 2: WHY DID GOD CREATE THE WORLD?

How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning: you have crashed to the earth, you who wounded the nations: who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the North; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High. In place of what we have translated, for ease of understanding, How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning, in the Hebrew, to render it word for word, one reads: How you have fallen from heaven, howl, son of the dawn. Now in other words Lucifer is meant; and he is told that he ought to weep and mourn, he who was once so glorious that he was compared to the brightness of the morning star. Just as, he says, the morning star, scattering the darkness, shines forth burning and ruddy, so your progress too among the peoples and in public seemed like a bright star; but you have fallen to the earth, you wounder of nations, who in your pride said: I have attained such power that heaven remains for me, and the stars, so that the things on high must lie beneath my feet. The Jews, however, would have heaven and the stars of God understood of themselves, on the strength of what follows: I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, that is, in the Temple, where the ordinances of God are laid up, and in the sides of the North, that is, in Jerusalem. For it is written: The mountains of Zion, the sides of the North (Ps 47 [48]:3). Nor had it been enough for his pride to desire heavenly things, unless he had burst out into such madness as to claim for himself the likeness of God.

[Daniel 4:4] "I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace." The narrative is clear indeed and requires but little interpretation. Because he displeased God, Nebuchadnezzar was turned into a madman and dwelt for seven years amongst the brute beasts and was fed upon the roots of herbs, Afterwards by the mercy of God he was restored to his throne, and praised and glorified the King of heaven, on the ground that all His works are truth and His ways are justice and He is able to abase those who walk in pride. But there are some who claim to understand by the figure of Nebuchadnezzar the hostile power which the Lord speaks of in the Gospel, saying: "I beheld Satan falling from heaven like lightning" (Luke 10:18). Likewise John in Revelation, in the passage where the dragon falls upon the earth drawing a third of the stars with him (Revelation 12:4). Likewise Isaiah: "How hath the morning star fallen, which used to rise early in the morning" (Isaiah 14:12). These authorities assert that it was absolutely impossible for a man who was reared in luxury to subsist on hay for seven years and to dwell among wild beasts for seven years without being at all mangled by them. Also they ask how the imperial authority could have been kept waiting for a mere madman, and how so mighty a kingdom could have gone without a king for so long a period. If, on the other hand, anyone had succeeded him on the throne, how foolish he would have to be thought to surrender an imperial authority which he had possessed for so long. Such a thing would be especially incredible since the historical records of the Chaldeans contain no such record, and since they recorded matters of far less import, it is impossible that they should have left things of major importance unmentioned. And so they pose all of these questions and offer as their own reply the proposition that since the episode does not stand up as genuine history, the figure of Nebuchadnezzar represents the devil. To this position we make not the slightest concession; otherwise everything we read in Scripture may appear to be imperfect representations and mere fables. For once men have lost their reason, who would not perceive them to lead their existence like brutish animals in the open fields and forest regions? And to pass over all other considerations, since Greek and Roman history offer episodes far more incredible, such as Scylla and the Chimaera, the Hydra and the Centaurs, and the birds and wild beasts and flowers and trees, the stars and the stones into which men are related to have been transformed, what is so remarkable about the execution of such a divine judgment as this for the manifestation of God's power and the humbling of the pride of kings? Nebuchadnezzar says, "'I was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace...'" or as Theodo-tion renders it "upon my throne." Now those who follow the interpretation we are opposing understand by the devil's home this world of ours. Concerning the world Satan himself in the Gospel says to the Savior: "All these things have been given over to me" (Luke 4:6). Likewise the Apostle says: "The world lieth in the Wicked One" (1 John 5:19).
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FOUR

Lucifer fell, Lucifer who used to rise at dawn; and he who was raised in a paradise of delight had the well-earned sentence passed upon him: "Though you exalt yourself as the eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, thence will I bring you down, says the Lord." For he had said in his heart, "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God," and "I will be like the Most High."

How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have crashed to the earth, you who wounded the nations? LXX: How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, who rose in the morning? He who sent to all the nations has been crushed to the earth. For Lucifer, who in Hebrew is called ELIL (הילל), Aquila translated howling son of the dawn. For truly he ought to howl and wail, who because of his pride was cast headlong from heaven to earth and crushed. Hence the Savior too says to the disciples: I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). Not, I see now; but I saw before, when he fell. And if he fell from so great a height because of pride, you too ought not to glory because the demons are subject to you, but because your names are written in heaven; so that whence he fell through pride, you may ascend through humility. This is the prince of the world, who rose in the morning among the other stars, and by his own fault was made from Lucifer into Vesper, and not rising but setting: who wounded the nations, or who sent his attendants to the nations, to deceive all by his fraud. These are the false apostles, deceitful workers, who transform themselves into Apostles of Christ, who sow darnel over the good seed while the teachers of the Churches sleep and are unwilling or unable to resist their malice. And Jacob, and Israel, on whom the Lord has had mercy and whom he has chosen, still says these things to the devil, or, as the Seventy will have it, about the devil, that is, not in the second person but in the third.

For example, what is said in Isaiah, "How he is fallen from heaven, Lucifer, son of the morning!" and the other statements in that context that speak of the king of Babylon are of course to be understood of the devil. However, the statement that is made in the same place, "He that sent orders to all nations is crushed on the earth," does not altogether fitly apply to the head himself.

A certain one was named Lucifer, who fell; for he was an angel and became a devil; and concerning him the Scripture said, "Lucifer, who did arise in the morning, fell" And why was he Lucifer? Because, being enlightened, he gave forth light. But for what reason did he become dark! Because he abode not in the truth.

And So we are clearly shown that out of that number of them some of the leaders fell, by the lamentations of Ezekiel and Isaiah, in which we know that the prince of Tyre or that Lucifer who rose in the morning is lamented with a doleful plaint: and of him the Lord speaks as follows to Ezekiel: "Son of man, take up a lamentation over the prince of Tyre, and say to him: Thus saith the Lord God: Thou wast the seal of resemblance, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty. Thou wast in the pleasures of the paradise of God: every precious stone was thy covering: the sardius, the topaz and the jasper, the chrysolyte and the onyx and the beryl, the sapphire and the carbuncle and the emerald: gold the work of thy beauty, and thy pipes were prepared in the day that thou wast created. Thou wast a cherub stretched out and protecting, and I set thee in the holy mountain of God, thou hast walked in the midst of the stones of fire. Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day of thy creation, until iniquity was found in thee. By the multitude of thy merchandise thy inner parts were filled with iniquity and thou hast sinned; and I cast thee out from the mountain of God, and destroyed thee, O covering cherub, out of the midst of the stones of fire. And thy heart was lifted up with thy beauty: thou hast lost thy wisdom in thy beauty, I have cast thee to the ground: I have set thee before the face of kings, that they might behold thee. Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thy iniquities and by the iniquity of thy traffic." Isaiah also says of another: "How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning? how art thou fallen to the ground, that didst wound the nations? and thou saidst in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds. I will be like the Most High."
The Second Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 8

And that we may understand the power of its awful tyranny we see that that angel who, for the greatness of his splendour and beauty was termed Lucifer, was cast out of heaven for no other sin but this, and, pierced with the dart of pride, was hurled down from his grand and exalted position as an angel into hell. If then pride of heart alone was enough to cast down from heaven to earth a power that was so great and adorned with the attributes of such might, the very greatness of his fall shows us with what care we who are surrounded by the weakness of the flesh ought to be on our guard. But we can learn how to avoid the most deadly poison of this evil if we trace out the origin and causes of his fall. For weakness can never be cured, nor the remedies for bad states of health be disclosed unless first their origin and causes are investigated by a wise scrutiny. For as he (viz., Lucifer) was endowed with divine splendour, and shone forth among the other higher powers by the bounty of his Maker, he believed that he had acquired the splendour of that wisdom and the beauty of those powers, with which he was graced by the gift of the Creator, by the might of his own nature, and not by the beneficence of His generosity. And on this account he was puffed up as if he stood in no need of divine assistance in order to continue in this state of purity, and esteemed himself to be like God, as if, like God, he had no need of any one, and trusting in the power of his own will, fancied that through it he could richly supply himself with everything which was necessary for the consummation of virtue or for the perpetuation of perfect bliss. This thought alone was the cause of his first fall. On account of which being forsaken by God, whom he fancied he no longer needed, he suddenly became unstable and tottering, and discovered the weakness of his own nature, and lost the blessedness which he had enjoyed by God's gift. And because he "loved the words of ruin," with which he had said,will ascend into heaven," and the "deceitful tongue," with which he had said of himself, "I will be like the Most High," and of Adam and Eve, "Ye shall be as gods," therefore "shall God destroy him forever and pluck him out and remove him from his dwelling place and his root out of the land of the living." Then the just, when they see his ruin, shall fear, and shall laugh at him and say" (what may also be most justly aimed at those who trust that they can obtain the highest good without the protection and assistance of God): "Behold the man that made not God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and prevailed in his vanity."
The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 12, Chapter 4

The first among the Angels, Lucifer, presuming upon his private good, sought private excellence, wishing to be raised above the others; and therefore he fell together with the rest who consented to him. Falling, moreover, he became impenitent, obstinate and blinded and excluded from the contemplation of God and disordered in operation, striving with all his effort to subvert man through manifold temptation. Since through the free choice of the will he could tend toward the supreme good or turn toward his private good, Lucifer, aroused by the consideration of his own beauty and loftiness to love himself and his own private good, presumed upon the loftiness he possessed and sought his own excellence, yet not one that was obtained; and by this, in presuming, he made himself his own principle, glorying in himself; and in seeking, he made himself his own supreme good, resting in himself. But since he was neither the supreme principle nor the supreme good, it was necessary that by his disordered ascent he should fall; and by equal reason, all who consented in this. And immediately when he fell into sin, together with the rest who adhered to him, he lost the highest place, namely the empyrean, descending to the lowest, namely the murky air or hell, so that the fall into guilt was through free choice, but the fall into punishment was through divine judgment.

Second, they reproach him with the glory he has lost. Both as to the dignity of the king: O Lucifer, beautiful among all other kings, in the morning, monarch before all others; and as to the power of war: how are you fallen to the earth: you, therefore, are the head of gold. And after you shall rise up another kingdom, inferior to you (Dan 2:38-39).

It is the prince of the world; but it is also a usurper. So he will apprehend vaguely what the vision will give to him vividly; no less than all that strange story of treason in heaven and the great desertion by which evil damaged and tried to destroy a cosmos that it could not create. It is a very strange story and its proportions and its lines and colours are as arbitrary and absolute as the artistic composition of a picture. It is a vision which we do in fact symbolise in pictures by titanic limbs and passionate tints of plumage; all that abysmal vision of falling stars and the peacock panoplies of the night. Good and evil, then, are not on all fours. Badness is not even bad in the same way in which goodness is good. Ormuzd and Ahriman cannot be equals. Now it is impossible at this point not to remember a certain sacred story which, though never included in the creeds, has been widely believed in the Church and seems to be implied in several Dominical, Pauline, and Johannine utterances--I mean the story that man was not the first creature to rebel against the Creator, but that some older and mightier being long since became apostate and is now the emperor of darkness and (significantly) the Lord of this world.

It seems to me, therefore, a reasonable supposition, that some mighty created power had already been at work for ill on the material universe, or the solar system, or, at least, the planet Earth, before ever man came on the scene: and that when man fell, someone had, indeed, tempted him. This hypothesis is not introduced as a general "explanation of evil": it only gives a wider application to the principle that evil comes from the abuse of free-will. If there is such a power, as I myself believe, it may well have corrupted the animal creation before man appeared.

And do you now begin to see why Christianity has always said that the devil is a fallen angel? That is not a mere story for the children. It is a real recognition of the fact that evil is a parasite, not an original thing. The powers which enable evil to carry on are powers given it by goodness. All the things which enable a bad man to be effectively bad are in themselves good things—resolution, cleverness, good looks, existence itself. That is why Dualism, in a strict sense, will not work.

If you mistake for your own merits what are really God's gifts to you through nature, and if you are contented with simply being nice, you are still a rebel: and all those gifts will only make your fall more terrible, your corruption more complicated, your bad example more disastrous. WHY WAS THE SON OF GOD SENT, AND NOT ANOTHER? — Although everything that God does must be believed to be done reasonably and providentially, I nevertheless think it better if, after faith, the cause of what is done can also be noticed, so that what is believed is not unknown. Therefore the Lord says: “Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (Jn. 17:3). For first what is said by the Prophet must be believed, and then what is believed must be known; because the Holy Spirit helps the faithful and diligent person in this matter, so that by coming to know he may understand the rationale of faith. Then he enjoys the full joy of his believing, if he understands what he believes. For this is the strength of faith, this the immovable foundation of belief: to learn the mystery. For where there is only faith, devotion is not so pure, and deception can gain entrance. Therefore the chosen vessel labors so that believers may learn the rationale of their faith. For when they have come to know how great he is in whom they have trusted, and what his power is, they will by no means and in no way allow themselves to be turned away from hope in him. Therefore we read the saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 34:9), so that by deliberate effort they may know the flavor of his divinity, understanding that nothing is wiser than to believe in Christ.
